acupoints.code: I.A.a.2. Index finger, palmar – Jianshang zone
acupoints.name: Dajian
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; branch nerves of the heart and the six bowels; branch nerve of the liver.
acupoints.location: Dajian: palm facing up, on the index finger's first segment, at its centre, 0.3 cun towards the outer side. Cejian: palm facing up, 0.25 cun below the point 0.3 cun lateral to the centre of the index finger's first segment — that is, 0.25 cun below Dajian. Xiaojian: palm facing up, above and lateral on the first segment of the index finger, 0.25 cun directly above Dajian.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Dajian: clears heart fire, drains lung heat, benefits the throat. Xiaojian: diffuses the lung and stops cough, reduces swelling and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Dajian: endocarditis, palpitations, cardiac asthma, hernia, tonsillitis, abdominal distension, trigeminal neuralgia, childhood asthma, childhood malnutrition, enteritis. Cejian: diffuses the lung and transforms phlegm, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, clears heat and relieves pain. Xiaojian: coughing yellow phlegm, bronchial asthma, chest oppression, palpitations, knee pain, hernia (particularly effective), small-intestine distension, keratitis, tonsillitis, childhood asthma, childhood malnutrition, enteritis.
acupoints.technique: Dajian: perpendicular insertion with a 0.5-cun needle, to a depth of 0.1–0.4 cun. At 0.1 cun the needle reaches the cardiac branch nerve; at 0.2–0.4 cun the liver and intestinal nerves. May also be pricked to bleed with a three-edged needle. Cejian: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.4 cun, or pricked to bleed with a three-edged needle — particularly effective for asthma, bronchitis and childhood pneumonia. Xiaojian: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.4 cun, or pricked to bleed, with the same effect as Dajian.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Local distension, soreness and an electric tingling.
acupoints.application: Needle the opposite side: for illness on the left, needle the right, and vice versa.
acupoints.notes: Dajian, Xiaojian and Waijian are all reaction points for the lung and airways in Master Tung's palm diagnosis. When a reaction shows at the point, needling it will be effective. This point enters the Heart channel shallowly, so a shallow insertion is enough. It can also treat asthma, though less effectively than Dingchuan or Shuangchuan. Master Tung said to take it on one hand only, but clinical experience finds no objection to taking it bilaterally. Cejian: not listed in Master Tung's book; it was made public in Master Hu's work. Its indications are broadly the same as Dajian. Tung's method often uses paired or adjacent needling to strengthen the effect, so in practice his students rarely use a single point alone — clinically, three of Dajian, Xiaojian, Zhongjian and Xiajian may be needled together. Xiaojian: in patients with hernia, when blue-green vessels appear on the airway and male genital areas of Tung's distinctive palm diagnosis, using the related points listed above is markedly effective for hernia.

acupoints.code: I.A.a.2. Index finger, palmar – Jianshang zone
acupoints.name: Zhongjian
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; branch nerves of the lung and heart; nerve of the six bowels.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, at the centre of the first segment of the index finger.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Regulates heart qi, loosens the chest and benefits the diaphragm.
acupoints.indications: Palpitations, hernia, chest oppression, knee pain, dizziness, aching eyes, blurred vision with back pain.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion with a 0.5-cun needle to a depth of 0.2–0.3 cun.

acupoints.code: I.A.a.5. Index finger, palmar – Mu zone
acupoints.name: Muyi
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; liver nerve.
acupoints.location: Mu er: palm facing up, at the centre of the first segment of the index finger, 0.3 cun to the inner side of Zhongjian. Muyi: palm facing up, 0.25 cun below Mu er. Musan: palm facing up, 0.25 cun above Mu er.
acupoints.meridian: Mu er: enters the Liver channel. Muyi and Musan: enter the Liver, Stomach and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Mu er: courses the liver and rectifies qi, quickens the blood and dispels wind. Muyi and Musan: drain liver and gallbladder heat, open constraint and free the orifices.
acupoints.indications: Mu er: irritability, exuberant liver fire, tight painful shoulders, pain below the right ribs, tight painful neck, high cholesterol, distending stomach pain. Muyi: bitter taste and tinnitus, exuberant liver fire, irritability, aching shoulders, pain below the right ribs, tight painful neck. Musan: bitter taste and tinnitus, exuberant liver fire, irritability, aching shoulders, pain below the right ribs, tight painful neck, high cholesterol, hypochondriac pain, distending and vexing stomach pain.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.4 cun.
acupoints.application: More effective taken bilaterally. Clinically, any one or two of Muyi, Mu er and Musan may be used; pricking to bleed is very effective for gastrointestinal distension and hypochondriac pain. Bilateral needling is not contraindicated.
acupoints.notes:
Muyi: the depth of insertion determines which channel is reached. Muyi, Mu er and Musan were set out by Master Hu; Master Tung's book illustrates two Mu points but describes only one in the text. All three may be needled with a 0.5-cun needle: shallow at 0.1 cun enters the Lung channel, deeper at 0.2–0.4 cun enters the Liver and Stomach channels. This too is particular to Tung's points — the channel reached often changes with the depth of insertion, and this deserves attention. There are three Mu points in all, and needling all three together as a dao ma set is very effective for pain below the right ribs; it also helps dry mouth and excess fire. Muyi, Mu er and Musan treat liver function; the Upper Three Huang points treat the substance of the liver itself.
Mu er: in Master Tung's writings the Mu points have a narrow range of indications; Master Hu widened it, and in Lai's book the Mu point is also called the common-cold point. Lai reports that it works well for tearing, sweating, checking sweat and colds, and that it can stop a runny nose within moments. This author considers that for a cold with runny nose, adding Sanchasan, Linggu and Dabai, plus the foot cold point, works better than the Mu point alone. On the holographic projection of the organs onto the body, the Mu point falls in the liver zone — hence its name — and it is therefore specifically effective for pain below the right ribs.
Musan: in Lai's account, the Mu points can treat eyes that tear easily and feel dry, and can also stop unresolved external wind and skin itching. Because this point enters the Liver channel and the eyes connect to the liver, these indications follow. This author considers that combining it with Tung's Upper Three Huang points (Tianhuang, Minghuang, Qihuang) and the Skin 1, 2 and 3 points on the ear works better still.

acupoints.code: I.A.b.4. Middle finger, palmar – Xinchang zone
acupoints.name: Xinchang yi
acupoints.anatomy: Xinchang er and san: proper palmar digital nerve; branch nerves of the heart and lung. Xinchang yi: proper palmar digital nerve; cardiac nerve; branch nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: Xinchang er: palm facing up, at the centre of the first segment of the middle finger, 0.3 cun to the inner side. Xinchang yi: palm facing up, 0.25 cun below the point 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the middle finger's first segment. Xinchang san: palm facing up, 0.25 cun above Xinchang er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Xinchang er and san: course heart qi, clear the pericardium, quiet the spirit. Xinchang yi: regulates the heart and calms the spirit, courses heart qi, clears the pericardium.
acupoints.indications: Rheumatic heart disease, palpitations, angina, myocardial infarction, lung cancer, tuberculosis, chest pain.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.4 cun, or pricked to bleed with a three-edged needle.
acupoints.application: Take bilaterally.
acupoints.notes:
In Master Tung's own book the Xinchang point is placed 0.2 cun lateral to the midline of the middle finger's first segment, but this does not match the point illustrations at the back of the book, which show it medially. Master Hu, taught directly by Master Tung, corrected it to 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the first segment. Master Tung's text was never revised, and the descriptions often diverge from the illustrations; many later books simply copy the original without correction, and the error has been passed along — which is regrettable.
For treating heart conditions, the most commonly used points are Xinling on the hand and Tongguan and Tongshan on the thigh. This point may be combined with those, and with bloodletting between the third to sixth thoracic vertebrae.
Master Tung's writings give two Xinchang points; Master Hu added a third. Xinchang works well for palpitations and tachycardia and is specifically effective for chronic cardiac enlargement. In this author's clinical experience, the Xinling 1, 2 and 3 points in Region 3-3 of Tung's system are more effective than Xinchang for heart conditions.

acupoints.code: I.A.b.2. Middle finger, palmar – Huoxing zone
acupoints.name: Huoxing shang
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; branch nerves of the heart and lung.
acupoints.location: Huoxing shang: palm facing up, at the centre of the first segment of the middle finger. Huoxing xia: palm facing up, at the centre of the second segment of the middle finger.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses the heart and regulates qi, loosens the chest and benefits the diaphragm.
acupoints.indications: Dizziness, palpitations, angina, cardiac asthma, valvular heart disease, chest pain, scapular pain, lung cancer, multiple myeloma, pain in both legs, frozen shoulder, hiccup, gastric ulcer, duodenal ulcer.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.application: May be taken bilaterally.
acupoints.notes:
On the palm, the middle finger belongs to the heart in Tung's palm diagnosis, so Huoxing shang, Huoxing xia and Xinchang are all key points for heart conditions. Clinically they are usually combined with Linggu and Dabai; a larger set treats not only the heart but also conditions of the chest and lung.
The Huoxing points were not published in Master Tung's writings and were made public by Master Hu. Clinically, taking a point between Huoxing shang and Huoxing xia — right at the crease between the first and second segments — makes a vertical dao ma set and strengthens the effect. The middle finger governs the heart, so many points on it treat heart conditions. Heart and lung share one zone, so points that treat the heart also treat the lung; for lung conditions, always add Linggu and Dabai.

acupoints.code: I.A.b.7. Middle finger, palmar – Pizhong zone
acupoints.name: Pizhong yi
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; median nerve; splenic nerve; branch nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: Pizhong yi: palm facing up, 0.25 cun below the centre of the second segment of the middle finger. Pizhong er: palm facing up, 0.25 cun above the centre of the second segment of the middle finger.
acupoints.meridian: Pizhong yi: enters the Spleen and Stomach channels. Pizhong er: enters the Spleen, Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Pizhong yi: regulates the spleen and stomach, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels. Pizhong er: fortifies the spleen and eliminates damp, loosens the chest and clears the lung.
acupoints.indications: Pizhong yi: splenic sclerosis, splenomegaly, hepatitis, gastrointestinal distension, chest pain, back pain, aching, numb, swollen and painful toes. Pizhong er: hepatitis, splenomegaly, stomach distension, aching toes, pneumonia, heart disease, back pain, chest pain.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.4 cun.
acupoints.application: May be taken bilaterally.
acupoints.notes: Because Master Tung's original work did not publish the Huoxing points, its point descriptions differ from Master Hu's, though the locations are in fact the same. The Pizhong points correspond to the spleen area of palm diagnosis: people with spleen problems usually show an abnormal skin tone on the palm or the fingers. Pizhong yi, Pizhong er and Huoxing xia together form a dao ma set. Tung's acupuncture emphasises hand-and-foot correspondence — fingers answer to toes, and needling both treats pain in the corresponding area.

acupoints.code: I.A.c.5. Ring finger, palmar – Chao zone
acupoints.name: Huanchao
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; accessory nerves of the liver and kidney.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, 0.5 cun lateral to the centre of the second segment of the ring finger.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Regulates menstruation and the belt vessel, diffuses and frees the lower burner.
acupoints.indications: Ovaritis, ovarian cyst, uterine cancer, uterine pain, irregular menstruation, red and white vaginal discharge, blocked fallopian tubes, malposition of the uterus, quieting the fetus, vaginitis, urethritis.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.application: Combine with the Fuke points for the full range of gynaecological conditions.
acupoints.notes: Huanchao combines well with Fengchao (lateral palm side of the first segment of the ring finger) and the five Fuke points. Adding Tongshen and Tongwei to the key gynaecological points helps quiet the fetus. During pregnancy, do not use dao ma needling and do not needle Linggu, Sanyinjiao, or points on the fingers, toes and soles where the sensation is strong, to avoid premature labour or miscarriage. For uterine fibroid or uterine cancer: combine this point with the foot Sanchong points, plus Fuke, the Upper Three Huang points and free-position needling, with bloodletting over the sciatic area of the buttock. Needling from the palm side is more painful; it may also be needled from the back of the hand. For red and white discharge: combine this point with the foot Mufu point and with Libai and Yunbai.

acupoints.name: Fuyuan yi
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; hepatic nerve; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Fuyuan er: palm facing up, 0.25 cun above Fuyuan yi. Fuyuan yi: palm facing up, 0.25 cun below the point 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the first segment of the ring finger. Fuyuan san: palm facing up, 0.25 cun above the point 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the first segment of the ring finger — that is, 0.25 cun above Fuyuan er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses the sinews and benefits the bones, disperses swelling and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Swollen painful sinews, bony enlargement, periostitis, spinal disc problems (bone spurs), sciatica, lower back pain.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.3 cun. Pricking with a three-edged needle to draw yellow fluid is particularly effective.
acupoints.application: Fuyuan combined with the Wuhu points and the Upper Three Huang points (Tianhuang, Minghuang, Qihuang) treats bony swelling throughout the body.
acupoints.notes: Master Tung's original illustration places Fuyuan on the medial side, while the text does not specify the medial aspect of the first segment and instead says 0.2 cun lateral to the midline of the ring finger, which is unclear. Master Hu corrected it to 0.3 cun medial on the first segment. For indications, Master Tung's book lists only the reduction of bony enlargement; Master Hu broadened the range from what he had been taught, making public some of what had not been transmitted openly. Regions 1-1 and 2-2 hold many key points for the spine, lumbar vertebrae and sciatic pain; taking two or three sets together will show results.

acupoints.name: Pianjian
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; hepatic nerve; splenic nerve.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, 0.5 cun medial to the centre of the second segment of the ring finger.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, relieves pain and disperses stasis.
acupoints.indications: Chronic hepatitis, shoulder and back pain, frozen shoulder, pain on the lateral back of the hand, neck pain.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.4 cun.
acupoints.application: For illness on the right take the left, and for illness on the left take the right.
acupoints.notes: Pianjian and Shizhen are points Master Tung did not publish. Both are remarkably effective for a crick in the neck; with no needle to hand, a toothpick can be used instead, and after stimulating the point ask the patient to move the neck — relief comes quickly.
configNotes: Combining this point with Linggu, Dabai and Zhongbai works better still.

acupoints.code: I.A.c.7. Ring finger, palmar – Muyan zone
acupoints.name: Muyan yi
acupoints.location: Muyan er: palm facing up, 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the second segment of the ring finger. Muyan yi: palm facing up, 0.25 cun below the point 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the second segment of the ring finger. Muyan san: palm facing up, 0.25 cun above Muyan er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver channel.
acupoints.properties: Drains liver and gallbladder heat, courses the liver and rectifies qi.
acupoints.indications: Asthma, hepatitis of various kinds, cirrhosis, ascites, leg cramps, pain in both flanks.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.application: Muyan yi, er and san have the same action as the Upper Three Huang points in Region 8-8, though the leg points are usually preferred and Muyan is used less often. In fact it also works well for liver conditions.
acupoints.notes:
In Master Tung's book, Muyan is placed 0.2 cun lateral to the midline of the second segment of the ring finger, while the illustrations at the back mark it medially. Master Hu corrected Muyan to 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the second segment, in keeping with what Master Tung transmitted. There are several asthma points on the fingers — Dajian, Xiaojian, Zhongjian, the two Shuangchuan points, the three Dingchuan points, and this one. This author considers that whichever of these shows a dark discoloured spot should be needled, and the effect will be there.
Among hand points that enter the Liver channel and treat liver disease there are Mu 1, 2 and 3; the Zhi Sanhuang points; and Muyan 1, 2 and 3. All three sets treat liver-related conditions, and the Zhi Sanhuang points have the widest range, also covering gynaecological conditions. Because hand needling is painful, the body's Upper Three Huang points are used more often in practice, and for liver disease the ear liver point is commonly added.
In our experience, Muyan with the ear liver zone plus Ganling and the Upper Three Huang points was used for hepatitis B: of 132 cases, 78 resolved and 18 showed no clear effect. Muyan with the Upper Three Huang points, Shuijin, Shuitong and the hepatitis point, together with regular bloodletting, was used for infectious hepatitis: 291 cases became negative for CCF and HAA within two months of continuous treatment. The same points were used in 11 cases of cirrhosis, of which 9 resolved; the rest required medication alongside.
For stomatitis and inflammation under the tongue: grind dried longan seed, licorice and borneol to a powder and apply to the affected area.

acupoints.name: Shizhen
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the proper palmar digital nerve; renal nerve; cranial nerve.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, 0.2 cun above the point 0.2 cun medial to the centre of the second segment of the little finger.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Bladder channel.
acupoints.properties: Diffuses and frees qi and blood, opens constraint and frees the orifices.
acupoints.indications: Crick in the neck; neck pain (particularly effective); dizziness and heaviness in the head from overwork of the mind.

Shizhen may be paired with Pianjian on the ring finger; if a needle isn't to hand, firm pressure with the fingernail also works. Shizhen with Pianjian and Shenguan often relieves a crick in the neck quickly. Jianning, Sanchong and Qihu may also be added, together with local bloodletting.

acupoints.indications: Sprain of the medial or lateral ankle.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.notes: Huailing was never published by either Master Tung or Master Hu and was transmitted only orally. Its position matches the ankle point on the thumb diagram in the palm-diagnosis material.

acupoints.code: I.P.e.5. Thumb – Fuke zone
acupoints.name: The five Fuke points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the proper palmar digital nerve; uterine nerve; nerve of the six bowels.
acupoints.location: On the back of the hand, on the lateral side of the first segment of the thumb, 0.25 cun from the midline. Starting at the metacarpophalangeal crease, one point every 0.2 cun upward to the crease of the second segment — five points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Ren and Du vessels.
acupoints.properties: Regulates menstruation and the belt vessel, diffuses and frees the lower burner.
acupoints.indications: Uterine fibroid, uterine cancer, metritis, ovaritis, infertility, menstrual pain, irregular menstruation, excessive or scanty menstruation, genital pain and swelling, red and white vaginal discharge, vaginal flatus, postpartum wind conditions.
acupoints.technique: 0.5-cun needle, perpendicular to 0.2–0.3 cun, or shallow pricking to bleed with a three-edged needle.
acupoints.application: The five Fuke points are among Tung's 72 principal needlings and are specifically effective across the full range of women's conditions. Clinically any two or three may be needled, with immediate results. For lower back ache or lower abdominal pain with menstruation, three of the Fuke points may be needled and retained.
acupoints.notes: The five Fuke points are the main points for the whole range of gynaecological conditions and are essential in gynaecological treatment. They may be combined with other related points such as Fengchao and Mufu. Combined with Menjin, the Upper Three Huang points and the Lower Three Huang points they are specifically effective for menstrual pain. Master Tung's book gives two Fuke points and Master Hu added three, making five; this author considers that three points in dao ma within this area is sufficient.

acupoints.code: I.P.z.3. Metacarpophalangeal joints – Muhuo zone
acupoints.name: The four Muhuo points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the proper palmar digital nerve; branch nerves of the heart and liver.
acupoints.location: As described above for Muhuo yi, er, san and si.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, quickens the blood and dispels stasis.
acupoints.indications: Hemiplegia, leg pain, sequelae of stroke, tinea pedis.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion from above downward at 15 degrees, to a depth of 0.1–0.2 cun. Shallow pricking to bleed is remarkably effective.
configNotes: This point is among Tung's 72 principal needlings and is specifically effective for hemiplegia; combined with the Baguan points the effect doubles.

acupoints.code: I.P.e.3. Thumb – Zhixian zone
acupoints.name: The five Zhixian points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial branch of the radial nerve; ocular nerve; gastric nerve.
acupoints.location: On the back of the hand, 0.5 cun medial to the midline of the thumb. Starting at the metacarpophalangeal crease, one point every 0.2 cun upward — five points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Supports the spleen and manages the blood, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: Drooling in children, drooling after stroke, cold stomach with stomach pain, deficiency diarrhoea, keratitis, conjunctivitis, optic neuritis, optic atrophy, cataract, tearing in the wind, toothache, intestinal hernia.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion from medial to lateral, 0.2–0.3 cun, or pricked to bleed.
acupoints.notes: Master Tung's book lists only two Zhixian points, located on the medial aspect of the first segment on the back of the thumb, 0.2 cun in from the midline; the illustration places them near the border between the darker and lighter skin. Master Hu corrected the location to 0.5 cun medial to the midline and divided it into five points. Master Tung once said that each finger forms a system in itself: the back of the thumb is a hologram of the whole body, and by reading head, chest, upper abdomen and lower abdomen you can find where Zhixian lies. The thumb with the first metacarpal is also a hologram of the body, in which the whole thumb represents the head — and Zhixian falls where the salivary glands are.

acupoints.code: I.P.e.4. Thumb – Zhiwu zone
acupoints.name: The Zhiwu points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the median nerve; renal nerve; splenic nerve.
acupoints.location: As described above for Zhiwu yi, er and san.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Disperses swelling and dispels stasis.
acupoints.indications: Long-standing malignant sores, malignant tumours; after surgery for an abscess or malignant tumour, a wound that discharges continuously and will not close or scab.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion from below upward, 0.1–0.2 cun, or pricking to release dark blood — effective at once.
acupoints.notes: The illustrations in Master Tung's book show three Zhiwu points but the text does not explain them clearly, saying only a few words about their being on the midline of the first segment on the back of the thumb, and omitting a good deal. Master Hu set out all three clearly.
configNotes: Combined with the Waisanguan and Shangliu points, this point works well for external tumours.

acupoints.code: I.P.a.5. Index finger, dorsal – Zhisima zone
acupoints.name: The Zhisima points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial branch below the median nerve; branch nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: As described above for Sima yi, er and san.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and releases the exterior, harmonises qi and blood.
acupoints.indications: Skin conditions, dark facial patches, freckles, rhinitis, tinnitus, otitis media, chest pain, pleurisy.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Zhisima, Zhiwujin and Zhiqianjin lie on the same line: Zhiwujin on the first segment of the back of the index finger, Zhisima on the second. Master Tung's original gives 0.2 cun lateral, while Master Hu's gives 0.3 cun — this is the difference between the two.

acupoints.code: I.P.b.2. Middle finger, dorsal – Dan zone
acupoints.name: The Dan points
acupoints.anatomy: Subcutaneous branch of the median nerve; gallbladder nerve; accessory cardiac nerve.
acupoints.location: As described above for Dan yi and Dan er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Gallbladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Settles, rectifies qi, relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Night crying in infants, abdominal distension, aching distended legs, neuralgia of the lower leg, dizziness, headache, jaundice, fright palpitations.
acupoints.technique: Dan yi: oblique insertion from medial to lateral, 0.2–0.3 cun. Dan er: oblique insertion from lateral to medial, 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.notes: For indications, Master Tung's original lists only fright of the heart and night crying in infants; Master Hu added a good deal more, making public much of the essence of Tung's points without holding back. Erjiaoming treats the lumbar vertebrae, while Dan may be combined with Wanshun yi, Sanhe and Fenshui for lower back pain. When chronic cholecystitis flares and causes epigastric or hypochondriac pain, the Dan points work well.

acupoints.code: I.P.b.1. Middle finger, dorsal – Erjiaoming zone
acupoints.name: Erjiaoming
acupoints.anatomy: Subcutaneous branch of the median nerve; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: On the back of the hand, on the longitudinal midline of the first segment of the middle finger: one point 0.3 cun from the crease of the second segment and one point 0.6 cun from it — two points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses qi and transforms stasis, disperses distension and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Distending pain from raised intraocular pressure, aching brow ridge, lower back pain, acute lumbar sprain, aching nasal bone.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion from above downward, 0.1–0.2 cun, or pricked to bleed with a three-edged needle.
acupoints.notes: Muhuo er, Feixin and Erjiaoming run down in a line that represents the spine, and also the Du vessel. On the middle finger, Erjiaoming falls at the position corresponding to the lumbar vertebrae, which is why it treats lower back pain and acute lumbar sprain.
configNotes: Erjiaoming is more effective for lower back pain arising from the lumbar vertebrae themselves; Wanshun, Fenshui and Sanhe may be added, together with bloodletting at the site.

acupoints.code: I.P.b.4. Middle finger, dorsal – Xinxi zone
acupoints.name: The Xinxi points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the median nerve; branch nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: As described above for Xinxi yi and Xinxi er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart channel.
acupoints.properties: Disperses swelling and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Scapular pain, neck pain, distending and aching pain in the lower leg, knee pain.
acupoints.technique: Xinxi yi: oblique insertion from medial to lateral, 0.2–0.3 cun. Xinxi er: oblique insertion from lateral to medial, 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.application: Taking both hands together is not contraindicated.
acupoints.notes: Master Tung's account differs: for location it says only the back of the middle finger, on either side of the centre of the second segment, without giving measurements. Master Hu specified them at 0.5 cun to the medial and lateral sides. When needling isn't convenient, firm pressure with the fingernail also works well.

acupoints.code: I.P.b.3. Middle finger, dorsal – Feixin zone
acupoints.name: The Feixin points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the median nerve; branch nerves of the heart and lung.
acupoints.location: As described above for Feixin yi, er and san.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Diffuses and frees qi and blood, frees the connecting vessels and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Cervical bone spurs, spinal bone spurs, tight painful neck, intercostal neuralgia, chest pain, back pain, neuralgia of the thumb, sciatica, occipital headache, lower leg pain.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion from above downward, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Feixin and Erjiaoming lie on one line. The back of the middle finger can be read as the back of the body, and the line connecting Muhuo er, Feixin and Erjiaoming as the spine and the Du vessel — which is why Feixin is effective for a tight painful neck, cervical bone spurs and spinal bone spurs.

acupoints.code: I.P.c.3. Ring finger, dorsal – Zhishen zone
acupoints.name: The Zhishen points
acupoints.anatomy: Ulnar nerve; accessory hepatic nerve; accessory renal nerve; cardiac nerve.
acupoints.location: As described above for Zhishen yi, er and san.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Regulates heart qi, enriches kidney yin.
acupoints.indications: Cardiac asthma, chest pain, kidney depletion, cardiac weakness, back pain, dry mouth.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Zhishen belongs to the Heart and Kidney channels and is therefore effective for conditions of both, working best for heart conditions accompanied by impaired kidney function such as kidney depletion. The kidney governs saliva, so points belonging to the kidney can treat dry mouth — for dry mouth: Shenguan, Shuijin, Shuitong. Master Tung's writings give 0.2 cun lateral, corrected in Master Hu's book to 0.3 cun. Needling close against the bone gives better results.
configNotes: For chest and back pain, use all three needles together; combined with Xinling on the hand this point is specifically effective for cardiac arrest; combined with Dizong it works remarkably for cardiac enlargement and pericardial effusion.

acupoints.code: I.P.e.2. Thumb – Zhuyuan zone
acupoints.name: The Zhuyuan points
acupoints.anatomy: Subcutaneous branch of the proper palmar digital nerve; nerves of the lung and kidney; ocular nerve.
acupoints.location: Zhuyuan yi: on the back of the thumb at the interphalangeal joint, 0.5 cun to the medial side of the crease. Zhuyuan er: on the back of the thumb at the interphalangeal joint, 0.5 cun to the lateral side of the crease.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and drains fire, enriches yin and brightens the eyes.
acupoints.indications: Cataract, glaucoma, keratitis, conjunctivitis, amblyopia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2–0.5 cun.
acupoints.notes: On the holographic map of the thumb, Zhuyuan falls at the position of the chest cavity, so needling a little to its medial side treats the chest point — in other words Zhuyuan lies close to the chest point. Zhuyuan can treat the whole range of eye conditions.

acupoints.code: I.P.c.4. Ring finger, dorsal – Zhisanzhong zone
acupoints.name: The Zhisanzhong points
acupoints.anatomy: Ulnar nerve; accessory hepatic nerve; accessory renal nerve.
acupoints.location: As described above for Zhisanzhong yi, er and san.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Quickens the blood and transforms stasis, courses wind and disperses swelling.
acupoints.indications: Mastitis, breast lump, swollen nipple, muscular atrophy, dispelling wind, facial nerve paralysis.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.application: Combined with Jianfeng it is specifically effective for breast cancer and breast lumps.
acupoints.notes: Master Tung's book locates the point 0.2 cun lateral to the midline of the middle segment of the ring finger without saying it is on the back of the finger — probably an omission. Master Hu revised it to 0.3 cun lateral, in keeping with what Master Tung taught.

acupoints.code: I.P.z.2. Metacarpophalangeal joints – Qihua zone
acupoints.name: Shaobai
acupoints.anatomy: Subcutaneous branch of the proper palmar digital nerve; branch nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: On the back of the hand at the proximal interphalangeal joint of the little finger, 0.3 cun medial to the centre of the crease.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, rectifies qi and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Lower back pain, bone spurs of the lumbar vertebrae, sciatica.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion, 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.notes: Shaobai does not appear in Master Tung's book and was first made public by Master Hu. It enters the Kidney channel, so it is effective only for lumbar spine pain, lower back pain and sciatica that arise from the kidney.

acupoints.code: I.A.b.7. Middle finger, palmar – Kaipi zone
acupoints.name: Kaipi
acupoints.anatomy: Proper palmar digital nerve; splenic nerve.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, at the exact centre of the third segment of the middle finger.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Regulates the spleen and stomach, diffuses and frees the middle burner.
acupoints.indications: No appetite, poor appetite, vomiting, chest oppression, dizziness.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Kaipi does not appear in Master Tung's own writings; the point was set out by Master Hu in his book on the basis of what Master Tung taught.

acupoints.code: I.A.d.3. Little finger, palmar – Fenshui zone
acupoints.name: The Fenshui points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Fenshui er: palm facing up, 0.3 cun lateral to the exact centre of the first segment of the little finger (the Taiyang yi point). Fenshui yi: 0.2 cun below Fenshui er. Fenshui san: 0.2 cun above Fenshui er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Regulates the lower burner, eliminates damp and drains turbidity, disinhibits water and disperses swelling.
acupoints.indications: Nephritis with oedema, tinnitus, deafness, herniated lumbar disc (bone spurs), lower back pain, sciatica.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Pain with slight soreness and distension.
acupoints.notes: Fenshui lies on the little finger, which belongs to the kidney; many points on the little finger and its metacarpal enter the Kidney channel. In Chinese medicine, therefore, bone and ear conditions related to the kidney all fall within the scope of the points in this area. Fenshui was first made public in Master Hu's book, on the basis of Master Tung's teaching.

acupoints.code: I.A.d.4. Little finger, palmar – Shuiqing zone
acupoints.name: The Shuiqing points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Shuiqing er: on the palmar side, 0.3 cun lateral to the exact centre of the second segment of the little finger. Shuiqing yi: 0.2 cun below Shuiqing er. Shuiqing san: 0.2 cun above Shuiqing er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney and Bladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses and drains reverting qi, disinhibits and guides the lower burner.
acupoints.indications: Orchitis, nephritis with oedema, urethritis, cystitis, migraine, lower back pain, leg pain.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Shuiqing does not appear in Master Tung's own book; Master Hu set it out in his writings on the basis of what Master Tung taught. Shuiqing and Fenshui lie on the same line on the little finger. Like Fenshui it enters the Kidney channel, but it also enters the Bladder channel, and so treats conditions of the bladder and urethra.

acupoints.code: I.A.d.6. Little finger, palmar – Shuihai zone (hand)
acupoints.name: The Shuihai points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Shuihai er: 0.3 cun medial to the exact centre of the second segment of the little finger. Shuihai yi: 0.2 cun below Shuihai er. Shuihai san: 0.2 cun above Shuihai er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Frees the connecting vessels and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Tight painful neck, back pain, lower back pain, sciatica.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Shuihai is not listed in Master Tung's own writings and was set out by Master Hu on the basis of what Master Tung taught. It enters the Kidney channel, yet it does not treat conditions of the kidney organ itself; it treats bone conditions of the back — which follows from the principle that the kidney governs the bones.

acupoints.code: I.A.d.5. Little finger, palmar – Shuiyuan zone
acupoints.name: The Shuiyuan points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial subcutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Shuiyuan er: 0.3 cun medial to the exact centre of the first segment of the little finger. Shuiyuan yi: 0.2 cun below Shuiyuan er. Shuiyuan san: 0.2 cun above Shuiyuan er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Frees the connecting vessels and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Numb hands, abdominal pain, bone spurs of the cervical vertebrae.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Shuiyuan does not appear in Master Tung's original work; Master Hu made it public in his writings on the basis of Master Tung's regular teaching. Shuihai and Shuiyuan lie on the same line on the palmar side of the little finger; both enter the Kidney channel and treat bone conditions.

acupoints.code: I.P.d.2. Little finger, dorsal – Shuiyao zone
acupoints.name: The Shuiyao points
acupoints.anatomy: Palmar branch of the ulnar nerve; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Shuiyao er: at the exact centre of the second segment on the back of the little finger. Shuiyao yi: 0.3 cun medial to Shuiyao er. Shuiyao san: 0.3 cun lateral to Shuiyao er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Frees the connecting vessels and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Lower back pain (particularly effective), sciatica, keratitis, conjunctivitis, distending pain from raised intraocular pressure, dizziness, migraine.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Shuiyao was first made public by Master Hu on the basis of Master Tung's regular teaching. Like Zhengshui it lies on the little finger and enters the Kidney channel — Zhengshui on the first segment, Shuiyao on the second — and for the most part their fields of treatment coincide.

acupoints.code: II.L.a.1. Lateral to the 1st and 2nd metacarpals – Lingbai zone
acupoints.name: Linggu
acupoints.anatomy: Linggu: superficially, the dorsal venous network of the hand and the superficial branch of the radial nerve; deeply, the proper palmar digital nerve of the median nerve, the branch nerve of the lung, and the nerves of the heart and kidney. Dabai: the radial artery, the radial nerve and the branch nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: Linggu: locate with the hand in a fist, in the web between thumb and index finger, at the junction of the first and second metacarpals. It may be threaded through to Zhongxian. Dabai: with the hand in a fist, between the first and second metacarpals, 1 cun distal to Linggu.
acupoints.meridian: Linggu: enters the Heart, Lung and Large Intestine channels. Dabai: enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Linggu: frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, diffuses the lung and regulates qi, frees and downbears the stomach and intestines, moves qi and quickens the blood to transform stasis. Dabai: promotes sweating and releases the exterior, clears the lung and loosens the chest, clears the upper burner, depurates the lung and courses the exterior, moves qi and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Linggu: conditions arising from insufficient lung qi, emphysema, lung cancer, sciatica, lower back pain, back pain, foot pain, facial nerve paralysis, hemiplegia, headache, irregular menstruation, menstrual pain, difficult labour, coronary heart disease, arrhythmia, angina, gastric and duodenal ulcer, enteritis and colitis, facial scarring, eye conditions, tinnitus, deafness. Dabai: headache, migraine, lung cancer, pneumonia, pleural effusion, sciatica, lower back pain, back pain. Also childhood asthma, high fever and acute pneumonia.
acupoints.technique: Linggu: perpendicular insertion, 1–2 cun; may be threaded through to Zhongxian, or inserted obliquely outward 2–3 cun. Dabai: perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.5 cun; combined with bloodletting on the back it is specifically effective for childhood asthma, high fever and pneumonia.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Linggu: local soreness, distension and numbness. Contraindicated in pregnancy — this point strongly contracts the uterus and may cause miscarriage. Dabai: soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.
acupoints.application: Dabai is also a key point for supplementing qi. Paired with Linggu its range is very wide and it is effective for any pattern of qi stagnation with blood stasis. Where there is qi stagnation and qi vacuity, blood stasis and blood stagnation follow. Both Linggu and Dabai should be needled deeply for the effect to be marked. Blood stasis in the upper burner gives rise to lung disease and chest bind; in the middle burner, to abdominal masses; in the lower burner, to lower abdominal pain and gynaecological conditions; in the channels and connecting vessels, to painful obstruction of the joints, rheumatic conditions and hemiplegia; and stasis held internally alters the temperament and becomes a nervous disorder. Linggu and Dabai are therefore used to free and supplement qi, and so to scatter stagnation and disperse stasis.
acupoints.notes: Linggu is among Tung's 72 principal needlings, a major point for moving qi and quickening the blood and a key point for supplementing qi. It connects with a hundred points; the conditions it treats vary with the angle and direction of insertion, so it can be used across the whole range of illness.

acupoints.name: Dabai
acupoints.anatomy: The radial artery, the radial nerve and the branch nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: With the hand in a fist, between the first and second metacarpals, 1 cun distal to Linggu.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Promotes sweating and releases the exterior, clears the lung and loosens the chest, clears the upper burner, depurates the lung and courses the exterior, moves qi and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Headache, migraine, lung cancer, pneumonia, pleural effusion, sciatica, lower back pain, back pain. Also childhood asthma, high fever and acute pneumonia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.5 cun; or combined with bloodletting on the back, which is specifically effective for childhood asthma, high fever and pneumonia.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.
acupoints.application: This is also a key point for supplementing qi. Paired with Linggu its range is very wide and it is effective for any pattern of qi stagnation with blood stasis. Where there is qi stagnation and qi vacuity, blood stasis and blood stagnation follow. Both Linggu and Dabai should be needled deeply for the effect to be marked. Blood stasis in the upper burner gives rise to lung disease and chest bind; in the middle burner, to abdominal masses; in the lower burner, to lower abdominal pain and gynaecological conditions; in the channels and connecting vessels, to painful obstruction of the joints, rheumatic conditions and hemiplegia; and stasis held internally alters the temperament and becomes a nervous disorder. Linggu and Dabai are therefore used to free and supplement qi, and so to scatter stagnation and disperse stasis.

acupoints.code: II.A.a.1. 2nd metacarpal, palmar – Zhongzi – Zhongxian zone
acupoints.name: Zhongzi
acupoints.anatomy: Zhongzi: the radial nerve, the radial artery and the branch nerve of the lung. Zhongxian: the superficial branch of the radial nerve, the median nerve, the branch nerve of the lung and the branch nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: Zhongzi: palm facing up, between the first and second metacarpals, 1 cun proximal to the web of the thumb. It connects with Dabai. Zhongxian: palm facing up, below the seam between the first and second metacarpals; it connects with Linggu on the back of the same hand.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and releases the exterior, clears and drains lung qi.
acupoints.indications: Pneumonia, lung cancer, emphysema, common cold, cough, asthma, palpitations, fever, laryngitis, back pain, chest pain, knee pain.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1–2 cun. For conditions in children, pricking to bleed with a three-edged needle is specifically effective.
acupoints.notes: Zhongzi and Zhongxian lie close to the traditional Lung channel of the fourteen channels and also enter the Lung channel, so like Yuji they treat conditions related to the lung. Zhongxian is rarely used on its own; Zhongzi and Zhongxian are usually needled together.

acupoints.name: Zhongxian
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial branch of the radial nerve, the median nerve, the branch nerve of the lung and the branch nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, below the seam between the first and second metacarpals; it connects with Linggu on the back of the same hand.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Clears and drains lung qi, courses wind and releases the exterior.
acupoints.indications: As for Zhongzi.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1–2 cun. For conditions in children, pricking to bleed with a three-edged needle is specifically effective.
acupoints.notes: Zhongxian is rarely used on its own; Zhongzi and Zhongxian are usually needled together.

acupoints.code: II.A.e.1. 1st metacarpal, palmar – Tushui zone
acupoints.name: The Tushui points
acupoints.anatomy: The needle passes through skin and subcutaneous tissue and, crossing the abductor pollicis, reaches the lateral side of opponens pollicis; branches of the median nerve, the branch nerve of the spleen and the branch nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: Tushui er: 1 cun proximal to the depression on the radial side of the first metacarpal of the thumb. Tushui yi: 0.5 cun below Tushui er. Tushui san: 0.5 cun above Tushui er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Regulates the spleen and stomach, regulates the middle burner, clears and diffuses lung qi, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: Acute and chronic gastritis, long-standing stomach conditions, cough, asthma, tonsillitis, aching swollen bones throughout the body, muscular pain on the inner side of both legs, periostitis, sciatica.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion along the underside of the bone, 0.5–1 cun.
acupoints.application: Taking the points on both hands works better still.

acupoints.code: II.P.c.1. Metacarpals, dorsal – Zhongbai – Xiabai zone
acupoints.name: Zhongbai
acupoints.anatomy: The dorsal venous network of the hand, the ulnar nerve and artery with their dorsal branches, and the branch nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: Zhongbai: with the hand in a fist, between the fourth and fifth metacarpals, 0.5 cun proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joint. Xiabai: with the hand in a fist, between the fourth and fifth metacarpals, 1.5 cun from the metacarpophalangeal joint — that is, 1 cun proximal to Zhongbai, and 0.5 cun below Yemen of the Hand Shaoyang channel. This point is not Yemen of the fourteen channels; its correct position is 0.5 cun below Yemen.
acupoints.meridian: Zhongbai: enters the Kidney and Bladder channels. Xiabai: enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, disinhibits water and disperses swelling, disinhibits and guides the lower burner.
acupoints.indications: Zhongbai: cystitis, acute and chronic pyelonephritis, sciatica, bone spurs, lower back ache and pain, back pain, dizziness, astigmatism, tinnitus from kidney vacuity, humming in the head, hardness of hearing, oedema of the four limbs, migraine, spondylitis, degenerative arthritis, lower leg pain, acute lumbar sprain, wrenched qi. Xiabai: as for Zhongbai, and additionally distending liver pain and sensitive teeth.
acupoints.technique: Zhongbai: perpendicular insertion, 0.5 cun. Xiabai: perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.8 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.
acupoints.notes: Zhongbai is also called Guimen. It is among Tung's 72 principal needlings and one of the important points of Tung's extraordinary points, with a very wide range of treatment. As it enters the Kidney channel it is often used for conditions of the skeleton. Xiabai is seldom used alone; it is usually needled together with Zhongbai, and combined with other points treating the five viscera and six bowels to strengthen the effect — for example with Wanshun for bone spurs and sciatica, and with the Lower Three Huang points (Tianhuang, Dihuang, Renhuang) for acute and chronic nephritis.
configNotes: Zhongbai combined with Xiabai is specifically effective for acute lumbar sprain and wrenched qi, bone spurs, sciatica and ear conditions.

acupoints.name: Xiabai
acupoints.anatomy: The dorsal venous network of the hand, the ulnar nerve and artery with their dorsal branches, and the crossing nerves of the liver and kidney.
acupoints.location: With the hand in a fist, between the fifth and fourth metacarpals, 1.5 cun from the metacarpophalangeal joint — that is, 1 cun proximal to Zhongbai, and 0.5 cun below Yemen of the Hand Shaoyang channel. This point is not Yemen of the fourteen channels; its correct position is 0.5 cun below Yemen.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Disinhibits water and disperses swelling, courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, disinhibits and guides the lower burner.
acupoints.indications: As for Zhongbai, and additionally distending liver pain and sensitive teeth.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.8 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.
acupoints.notes: Xiabai is seldom used alone; it is usually needled together with Zhongbai, and combined with other points treating the five viscera and six bowels to strengthen the effect — for example with Wanshun for bone spurs and sciatica, and with the Lower Three Huang points (Tianhuang, Dihuang, Renhuang) for acute and chronic nephritis.

acupoints.code: II.P.b.1. Metacarpals, dorsal – Neibai – Waibai zone
acupoints.name: Neibai
acupoints.anatomy: The dorsal digital veins, the dorsal digital branches of the ulnar and radial nerves, the dorsal metacarpal artery and the splenic nerve.
acupoints.location: Neibai: with the hand in a fist, between the third and fourth metacarpals, 0.5 cun proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joint. Waibai: with the hand in a fist, between the third and fourth metacarpals, 1.5 cun proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joint — that is, 1 cun proximal to Neibai.
acupoints.meridian: Neibai: enters the Lung and Spleen channels. Waibai: enters the Lung and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Neibai: courses wind and releases the exterior, clears heat and resolves toxin, disperses swelling and relieves pain. Waibai: courses wind and releases the exterior, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: Neibai: chronic pancreatitis, splenomegaly, glomus lumps, swollen painful teeth, gingivitis, lower back pain, sciatica, allergic skin conditions, urticaria, vitiligo, purpura. Waibai: as for Neibai, and additionally trigeminal neuralgia, neuralgia of the mouth and teeth, and intercostal neuralgia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.8 cun.
acupoints.application: Waibai: for skin conditions, combine with the Sima points for a marked effect; for neuralgia, adding Waibai works remarkably well.
acupoints.notes: Neibai and Waibai are not explicitly listed in Master Tung's own book; Master Hu made public in his Complete Practical Collection of Master Tung's Extraordinary Acupuncture Points what Master Tung had taught but not set down in writing.

acupoints.name: Waibai
acupoints.anatomy: The dorsal digital veins, the superficial dorsal branches of the ulnar and radial nerves, the dorsal metacarpal artery and the splenic nerve.
acupoints.location: With the hand in a fist, between the third and fourth metacarpals, 1.5 cun proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joint — that is, 1 cun proximal to Neibai.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and releases the exterior, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: As for Neibai, and additionally trigeminal neuralgia, neuralgia of the mouth and teeth, and intercostal neuralgia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.8 cun.
acupoints.application: For skin conditions, combine with the Sima points for a marked effect; for neuralgia, adding Waibai works remarkably well.
acupoints.notes: Waibai is not explicitly listed in Master Tung's own book; Master Hu made public in his Complete Practical Collection of Master Tung's Extraordinary Acupuncture Points what Master Tung had taught but not set down in writing.

acupoints.code: II.P.a.1. Metacarpals, dorsal – Shangbai – Fenbai zone
acupoints.name: Shangbai
acupoints.anatomy: Crossing nerves of the heart and lung; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Shangbai: with the hand in a fist, between the second and third metacarpals, 0.5 cun proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joint. Fenbai: 1 cun proximal to Shangbai.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart, Lung and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and drains fire, enriches yin and brightens the eyes, frees the channels and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Shangbai: conjunctivitis, keratitis, sore distended eyes, myopia, astigmatism, angina, amblyopia, tearing in the wind, back pain, lower back pain, sciatica. Fenbai: combined with Shangbai it works remarkably for the whole range of eye conditions.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.8 cun.
acupoints.application: Taking the points on both hands works well.
acupoints.notes: In practice Shangbai and Fenbai are mostly used together, forming a dao ma needling. Fenbai does not appear in Master Tung's own book and was made public by Master Hu in his writings. Its indications are the same as Shangbai's, and the point combinations listed under Shangbai apply to both.

acupoints.name: Fenbai
acupoints.anatomy: Crossing nerves of the heart and lung; renal nerve.
acupoints.location: As described above for Fenbai.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart, Lung and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and drains fire, enriches yin and brightens the eyes.
acupoints.indications: As for Shangbai.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.8 cun.
acupoints.application: Combined with Shangbai this point works remarkably for the whole range of eye conditions.
acupoints.notes: In practice Shangbai and Fenbai are mostly used together, forming a dao ma needling. Fenbai does not appear in Master Tung's own book and was made public by Master Hu in his writings. Its indications are the same as Shangbai's, and the point combinations listed under Shangbai apply to both.

acupoints.code: II.L.a.2. Lateral to the 1st and 2nd metacarpals – Zhongkui zone
acupoints.name: Zhongkui
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial branch of the radial nerve; superficial branch of the median nerve; branch nerves of the heart and lung.
acupoints.location: Locate with the hand in a fist. As described above for Zhongkui.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Clears heat and brings down fever, diffuses the lung and stops cough.
acupoints.indications: Cough, asthma, trigeminal neuralgia, red swollen painful eyes, high blood pressure, anaesthesia for tooth extraction, fever with the common cold, headache, migraine.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion close against the underside of the bone, 0.2–0.5 cun; or pricked to bleed with a three-edged needle.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness and distension. This is also a key point for surgical anaesthesia.
acupoints.application: This is a key point for the common cold with high fever, and it also helps eye conditions and styes. For high blood pressure each needling lowers the pressure by 2–5 mmHg. For anaesthesia in tooth extraction it is threaded through to Dabai.

acupoints.code: II.A.c.3. 4th metacarpal, palmar – Shoujie zone
acupoints.name: Shoujie
acupoints.anatomy: Sensitive nerves of the five viscera; median nerve.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up. As described above for Shoujie.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart channel.
acupoints.properties: Harmonises qi and blood, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, settles and calms the spirit.
acupoints.indications: Resolves fainting from needling, and numbness or pain at the needle site arising after insertion; stabbing pain from disordered qi and blood, sciatica, lower back pain, trigeminal neuralgia, generalised pain, post-operative wound pain. It also resolves food poisoning and drug poisoning, and unbearable pain from acute gastroenteritis; and gives anaesthesia and pain relief for tooth extraction and for uterine surgery. The two points can also treat gallbladder conditions, gallstones, cholecystitis and nerve paralysis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2–0.8 cun. Relief comes the moment the needle goes in, or by pricking to bleed with a three-edged needle.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness, pain and an electric sensation.
acupoints.notes: Shoujie is one of Tung's 32 resolving points and an important point among Tung's extraordinary points; it works with remarkable speed and is the finest of the pain-relieving points. Of Shoujie yi and er, either one alone is enough. Like Shanggao and Xiagao, Shoujie also has a height-increasing effect. Zhengjin, Zhengzong, Zhenjing, Zhenghui, Sansheng, and the endocrine and testis points on the ear may be added. Shoujie is markedly effective for cramp in the opposite leg. Pinching Shoujie with one hand while striking Huofuhai firmly with the other treats aching and cramping of the opposite lower leg and discomfort after needling.

acupoints.code: II.A.c.4. 4th metacarpal, palmar – Gao zone
acupoints.name: Shanggao and Xiagao
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial branch of the median nerve; branches of the ulnar nerve; renal and cerebral nerves.
acupoints.location: Between the fourth and fifth metacarpals of the palm. Shanggao is 0.5 cun proximal to Shoujie er; Xiagao is 1.5 cun proximal to Shoujie er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses the channels and regulates qi, supplements the kidney and harmonises the stomach.
acupoints.indications: Pleurisy, peritonitis, appendicitis, ovaritis, acute and chronic enteritis of the small intestine, increasing height.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2–0.8 cun.
acupoints.application: Shanggao and Xiagao are among Tung's 72 principal needlings, and together they are specifically effective for peritonitis. They also stimulate secretion from the pituitary, of growth hormone, and from the cerebral cortex, and so can increase height: about twenty needlings may add 5–10 cm, with roughly a 60% chance of success. After the age of twenty the effect is smaller; it is best between sixteen and twenty.
acupoints.notes: This point lies on the same line as Shoujie, which also has a height-increasing effect. It is not listed in Master Tung's own book; Master Hu made it public in his writings on the basis of Master Tung's regular teaching.

acupoints.code: II.A.c.1. 4th metacarpal, palmar – Sanhe zone
acupoints.name: The Sanhe points
acupoints.anatomy: Superficial branch of the median nerve; nerve of the six bowels.
acupoints.location: As described above for Sanhe.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, moves qi and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Uterine pain, lower abdominal pain, sciatica, pain in both legs, bone spurs on the vertebrae, gallbladder conditions.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2–0.4 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle.
acupoints.application: Sanhe is specifically effective for lower back pain and sciatica.
acupoints.notes: Tung's extraordinary points are most often grouped in threes, and two or three needles are commonly inserted in succession — a method called dao ma needling, whose rationale is that two or three needles work better than one. Sanhe lies between the liver and kidney zones of palm diagnosis, which shows that it is closely related to both sinew and bone, and its field of treatment is correspondingly sinew- and bone-related. Sanhe is often paired with Wanshun to treat sciatica and bone spurs on the vertebrae.

acupoints.code: II.A.z.1. Carpals, palmar – Shouguan zone
acupoints.name: Guguan
acupoints.anatomy: Guguan: the median nerve, the renal nerve and the branch nerve of the lung. Muguan: the median nerve, the renal nerve and the nerves of the liver and gallbladder.
acupoints.location: Guguan: palm facing up, 0.5 cun distal to the midpoint of the transverse wrist crease and 0.5 cun toward the radial side, below the scaphoid — that is, 0.5 cun below the point where the line rising from the web between index and middle finger meets the wrist crease. Muguan: palm facing up, 0.5 cun distal to the midpoint of the transverse wrist crease and 0.5 cun toward the ulnar side — that is, 0.5 cun below and 0.5 cun ulnar to where the line rising from the web between middle and ring finger meets the wrist crease.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Drains the liver and resolves toxin, courses the channels and settles pain.
acupoints.indications: Guguan: hemiplegia, sciatica, nerve pain from vertebral overgrowth pressing on a nerve, duodenitis, resolving uric acid toxicity, food poisoning, drug poisoning. Muguan: lower back pain with chest oppression, pain in both flanks, jaundice, sciatica, leg pain, peritonitis, generalised joint pain, resolving uric acid toxicity, food poisoning, drug poisoning.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun.
acupoints.application: Muguan combined with Linggu, Xiabai and Guguan treats lower back pain, sciatica and bone spurs. It is particularly effective for bone and muscle pain arising from raised uric acid.
acupoints.notes: Guguan and Muguan are usually used together. Both are major, essential points in Tung's acupuncture, yet neither was included in Master Tung's own writings; Master Hu made public what Master Tung had taught by including them in his Complete Practical Collection of Master Tung's Extraordinary Acupuncture Points. Master Tung transmitted what are called the 72 principal needlings (the specifically effective needlings) and the 32 resolving needlings — Guguan and Muguan belong to both, which shows how important they are.

acupoints.name: Muguan
acupoints.anatomy: The median nerve, the renal nerve and the nerves of the liver and gallbladder.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, 0.5 cun distal to the midpoint of the transverse wrist crease and 0.5 cun toward the ulnar side — that is, 0.5 cun below and 0.5 cun ulnar to where the line rising from the web between middle and ring finger meets the wrist crease.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Drains the liver and resolves toxin, courses the channels and settles pain.
acupoints.indications: Lower back pain with chest oppression, pain in both flanks, jaundice, sciatica, leg pain, peritonitis, generalised joint pain, resolving uric acid toxicity, food poisoning, drug poisoning.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2–0.5 cun.
acupoints.application: This point combined with Linggu, Xiabai and Guguan treats lower back pain, sciatica and bone spurs. It is particularly effective for bone and muscle pain arising from raised uric acid.

acupoints.code: II.M.d.1. 5th metacarpal, palmar-medial – Wanshun zone
acupoints.name: Wanshun yi
acupoints.anatomy: At the abductor digiti minimi; the dorsal carpal artery and its branches, the ulnar nerve and the branch nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: Wanshun yi: on the lateral aspect of the back of the hand, on the ulnar side of the fifth metacarpal, 1.5 cun from the transverse wrist crease. Wanshun er: 1 cun distal to Wanshun yi.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Enriches the kidney and disinhibits urination, frees the kidney and settles pain.
acupoints.indications: Headache and blurred vision from kidney depletion, sciatica, pyelitis, nephritis, cystitis, lower back pain with swollen bones in the four limbs, back pain, bone spurs, pain in both legs, tinnitus, bone spurs of the neck. It also works remarkably for nosebleed and for a crick in the neck.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1 cun.
acupoints.application: Wanshun yi and er are specifically effective for bone conditions and kidney conditions. Taking the points on both hands works better still. The point 0.5 cun proximal to Wanshun yi is Wanshun shang, effective for coccygeal pain; the point 0.5 cun distal to Wanshun er, near Houxi, may serve as Wanshun xia, effective for cervical pain. For sciatica: Sanhe, Wanshun, Huoying, together with guided qi movement. For tinnitus: Wanshun, Sima, Sanzhong, Shenguan. For blurred vision from kidney depletion: Sancha yi, Wanshun yi.

acupoints.name: Wanshun er
acupoints.anatomy: The abductor digiti minimi, the dorsal carpal artery and its branches, the ulnar nerve and the branch nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: 1 cun distal to Wanshun yi.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Enriches the kidney and disinhibits urination, frees the kidney and settles pain.
acupoints.indications: As for Wanshun yi; it also works remarkably for nosebleed and for a crick in the neck.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1 cun.
acupoints.application: Wanshun yi and er are specifically effective for bone conditions and kidney conditions. Taking the points on both hands works better still. The point 0.5 cun proximal to Wanshun yi is Wanshun shang, effective for coccygeal pain; the point 0.5 cun distal to Wanshun er, near Houxi, may serve as Wanshun xia, effective for cervical pain.

acupoints.code: II.P.z.1. Metacarpals, dorsal – Sancha zone
acupoints.name: Sancha yi
acupoints.anatomy: Sancha yi: superficial branch of the radial nerve, the branch nerve of the lung and the accessory renal nerve. Sancha er: dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve, the splenic nerve and the branch nerve of the liver. Sancha san: dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve and the renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Sancha yi: at the centre of the web between the index and middle fingers. Sancha er: at the centre of the web between the middle and ring fingers. Sancha san: at the centre of the web between the little and ring fingers.
acupoints.meridian: Sancha yi: enters the Kidney channel. Sancha er: enters the Spleen and Liver channels. Sancha san: enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Sancha yi: enriches the kidney and settles pain, boosts the kidney and brightens the eyes. Sancha er: fortifies the spleen and transforms damp, moves qi and quickens the connecting vessels to transform stasis. Sancha san: enriches the kidney and settles pain, boosts the kidney and disinhibits urination.
acupoints.indications: Sancha yi: keratitis, sore aching eyes, lower back pain, sciatica, aching brow ridge, distending pain, optic atrophy, hemiplegia, wilting patterns. Sancha er: pancreatitis, splenomegaly, hemiplegia, sciatica, numbness of the hands and feet, hepatitis. Sancha san: dizziness and heaviness of the head, sciatica, bone spurs, lower back ache, lower back pain, pyelitis, kidney disease with oedema, severe common cold.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 2 cun. Make a fist and insert from the web. Sancha yi: insert from the web as far as the space between the two metacarpals. Sancha er: insert from the web to the upper border of the seam between the metacarpals. Sancha san: insert from the web straight to the upper border of the web between the metacarpals.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Local soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.
acupoints.application: Common cold with fever — severe cases: Sancha, Linggu, Dabai, Shen'er shang/zhong/xia, combined with bloodletting at the eighteen star points; Zhongzi and Zhongxian may be added. Mild cases: Linggu, Dabai, Zhongzi, Zhongxian. Amblyopia and optic atrophy: Sancha yi, Shenguan, Zhuyuan.
acupoints.notes: Sancha yi, er and san are not listed in Master Tung's own book; Master Hu made public what Master Tung taught by including them in his Complete Practical Collection of Master Tung's Extraordinary Acupuncture Points. The Sancha points can raise immunity and are essential points of remarkable effect among Tung's transmissions. There are three of them, each belonging to a different channel, and each has the power to regulate, supplement and drain the channel it enters — points Master Tung used constantly.

acupoints.name: Sancha er
acupoints.anatomy: Dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve, the splenic nerve and the branch nerve of the liver.
acupoints.location: At the centre of the web between the middle and ring fingers.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Liver channels.
acupoints.properties: Fortifies the spleen and transforms damp, moves qi and quickens the connecting vessels to transform stasis.
acupoints.indications: Pancreatitis, splenomegaly, hemiplegia, sciatica, numbness of the hands and feet, hepatitis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 2 cun, from the web to the upper border of the seam between the metacarpals. Make a fist and insert from the web.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.

acupoints.name: Sancha san
acupoints.anatomy: Dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve and the renal nerve.
acupoints.location: At the centre of the web between the little and ring fingers.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Enriches the kidney and settles pain, boosts the kidney and disinhibits urination.
acupoints.indications: Dizziness and heaviness of the head, sciatica, bone spurs, lower back ache, lower back pain, pyelitis, kidney disease with oedema, severe common cold.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 2 cun, from the web straight to the upper border of the web between the metacarpals. Make a fist and insert from the web.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.

acupoints.code: III.L.1. Forearm, lateral – Sanqi zone
acupoints.name: Qimen, Qijiao and Qizheng
acupoints.anatomy: Radial nerve, median nerve, branch nerve of the lung, nerve of the six bowels.
acupoints.location: Qimen: with the back of the hand up and the thumb web uppermost, on the upper border of the radius, 2 cun above the midpoint of the transverse wrist crease and 1 cun toward the radial side. For the others see the individual point entries.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Large Intestine and Bladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Moves qi and guides out stagnation, clears and drains the lower burner.
acupoints.indications: Metritis, ovaritis, irregular menstruation and other gynaecological conditions, red vaginal discharge, rectal prolapse, constipation, diarrhoea, uterine fibroid, cervical cancer, urethritis, cystitis, painful haemorrhoids, lower abdominal pain.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion is ineffective. Insert obliquely outward, roughly parallel to the skin at about 15 degrees, to 1.5 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness and distension with slight numbness.

acupoints.code: III.A.1. Forearm, anterior – Xinling zone
acupoints.name: Xinling yi, Xinling er and Xinling san
acupoints.anatomy: Between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus; superficially the medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm, deeply the median nerve and the branch nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: Palm facing up, Xinling yi is 1.5 cun above the midpoint of the transverse wrist crease, 0.5 cun from Neiguan. Xinling er is 1 cun above yi, and Xinling san 1 cun above er. Take them between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Pericardium channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees the connecting vessels of the heart, loosens the chest and scatters stagnation.
acupoints.indications: Arrhythmia, endocarditis, angina, cardiac enlargement, myocardial infarction, chest oppression, chest pain, epigastric pain, leg pain, frontal headache, dizziness, numbness of the hands and feet, sore throat.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.5 cun; the needle may also be threaded through to the back of the hand. Oblique insertion at 15 degrees from below upward treats heart disease. Oblique insertion at 30 degrees from below upward to 1.5 cun treats conditions of the chest and head. Oblique insertion at 45 degrees from above downward treats conditions of the hands and feet.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness and distension with slight numbness.
acupoints.notes: These three points are among Tung's 72 principal needlings and are essential points among Tung's extraordinary points. They were omitted from Master Tung's writings and supplied by Master Hu in his book. Note carefully that the depth and direction of insertion at Xinling change what the point treats.

acupoints.code: III.P.1. Forearm, posterior – Shouhuo zone
acupoints.name: Huochuan, Huoling and Huoshan
acupoints.anatomy: Superficially, branches of the cephalic vein and branches of the posterior and anterior cutaneous nerves of the forearm; deeply, the interosseous artery and vein and the posterior interosseous nerve, the branch nerve of the lung and the accessory cardiac nerve.
acupoints.location: Huochuan: with the back of the hand up and the arm extended level, 2.5 cun above the midpoint of the transverse wrist crease — that is, 0.5 cun above Waiguan. For the others see the individual point entries.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Triple Burner channel.
acupoints.properties: Diffuses and guides qi and blood, frees the connecting vessels and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Chest pain, back pain, hardness of hearing, chest oppression, pain in the forearm, pain on the front of the lower leg.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.5 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness and distension, sometimes spreading up and down to the fingers or the tip of the shoulder.
acupoints.notes: Huochuan, Huoling and Huoshan lie on the Triple Burner channel, which is interior–exterior paired with the Pericardium channel; needling all three together therefore treats chest pain, chest oppression and back pain. Needled deeply, Huoshan threads through to Celuoling, so besides sharing the indications of the other two it also treats pyelitis, lower back ache and sciatica.

acupoints.code: III.P.1. Forearm, lateral – Shouhuo zone
acupoints.name: Huofuhai
acupoints.anatomy: Superficially, branches of the cephalic vein and the posterior and anterior cutaneous nerves of the forearm; deeply, branches of the radial nerve, the branch nerve of the lung and the accessory cardiac nerve.
acupoints.location: Locate with the hand resting on the chest, between the radius and ulna, 2.5 cun below the transverse elbow crease — that is, 0.5 cun below and 0.5 cun lateral to Shousanli.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Dispels wind and depurates the lung, supplements and boosts kidney water.
acupoints.indications: Cough, asthma, common cold, rhinitis, sciatica, aching legs, lower back pain, anaemia, dizziness, blurred vision, excessive fatigue.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1 cun.
