acupoints.notes: Tongxin, Tongling, Tongguan, Tongshan and Tongtian are the five most important points for heart disease; they may also be used for everyday health maintenance and to strengthen circulatory function.

acupoints.code: VIII.A.4. Thigh, anterior – Jiemei zone
acupoints.name: Jiemei yi and Jiemei er
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, nerve of the six bowels, branch nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: Jiemei yi lies 1 cun medial to Tongshan and then 1 cun directly above; Jiemei er is 2.5 cun above it. Jiemei san is 2.5 cun directly above Jiemei er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver, Kidney, Spleen and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Jiemei yi and er: regulate menstruation and rectify qi, soothe the liver and resolve constraint. Jiemei san: soothes the liver and fortifies the spleen, harmonises the centre and transforms stagnation.
acupoints.indications: Uterine fibroid, metritis, uterine itching, blocked fallopian tubes, ovaritis, irregular menstruation, absence of menstruation (amenorrhoea), intestinal pain, gastric bleeding.
acupoints.technique: Jiemei yi and er: perpendicular insertion, 1.5–3 cun. Jiemei san: perpendicular insertion, 1.5–2.5 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Jiemei yi and er: soreness, numbness and distension. Jiemei san: soreness and distension.
acupoints.application: Needling Jiemei is awkward, as the points lie high on the inner thigh, and the Fuke points on the hand are now mostly used instead.
acupoints.notes: On the holographic projection of the viscera and bowels onto the body, the knee is the head and the groin is the groin, so Jiemei falls in the lower abdominal region — which is why it treats conditions related to the lower abdomen, such as intestinal pain and gynaecological conditions. This is one of the deeper principles of Tung's acupuncture and repays careful thought. Jiemei and Ganmao lie near the groin and near the Spleen and Liver channels, and so act positively on conditions of the reproductive system: they are close to the site of the problem and they treat along the channel, and their results are correspondingly good.

acupoints.name: Jiemei san
acupoints.anatomy: As for Jiemei yi.
acupoints.location: 2.5 cun directly above Jiemei er.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver, Kidney, Spleen and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Soothes the liver and fortifies the spleen, harmonises the centre and transforms stagnation.
acupoints.indications: As for Jiemei yi.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1.5–2.5 cun.
acupoints.notes: Jiemei and Ganmao lie near the groin and near the Spleen and Liver channels, and so act positively on conditions of the reproductive system: they are close to the site of the problem and they treat along the channel, and their results are correspondingly good.

acupoints.code: VIII.A.5. Thigh, anterior – Ganmao zone
acupoints.name: Ganmao yi and Ganmao er
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, nerve of the six bowels, branch nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: Ganmao yi is 1 cun medial to Jiemei er. Ganmao er is 1 cun medial to Jiemei san.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Spleen channels.
acupoints.properties: Clears heat and eliminates damp, diffuses the lung and dispels wind.
acupoints.indications: Severe common cold, high fever, influenza, chills and aversion to cold, headache with the common cold.
acupoints.technique: Needle to a depth of 1–2 cun, perpendicular or oblique.
acupoints.notes: Besides entering the Lung channel and treating conditions related to the common cold, Ganmao lies near the groin and near the Spleen and Liver channels; combined with the Lower Three Huang points it is also of considerable help in men's conditions.

acupoints.code: VIII.A.6. Thigh, anterior – Tongshui zone
acupoints.name: Tongshen
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Tongshen: in the depression at the upper medial border of the patella. Tongwei: 2 cun directly above Tongshen. Tongbei: 4 cun directly above Tongshen — that is, 2 cun above Tongwei.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Tongshen: diffuses and frees the lower burner, regulates menstruation and checks discharge. Tongwei: fortifies the spleen and harmonises the stomach, enriches yin and subdues yang. Tongbei: secures the kidney and banks up the origin, warms the channels and scatters cold.
acupoints.indications: Tongshen: pyelonephritis, chronic nephritis, diabetes, gonorrhoea, impotence, premature ejaculation, cystitis, metritis, red and white vaginal discharge, dizziness from kidney depletion, lower back pain, rheumatic kidney disease, high blood pressure, gastroenteritis, proteinuria, dry throat with oedema. Tongwei: as for Tongshen, and also back pain, stomach pain and pain in the forearm. Tongbei: as for Tongshen, and also headache, dizziness, back pain and fatigue.
acupoints.technique: Tongshen: perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1 cun. Tongwei: perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.5 cun; for dry mouth, perpendicular to 0.2 cun. Tongbei: perpendicular insertion, 1–2 cun; perpendicular to 0.3 cun resolves dry mouth at once.
acupoints.application: Master Tung says in his book that any one of Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei may be taken as a supplementing needling to treat miscarriage in women; half a month of continuous treatment removes the risk of miscarriage. Only one point may be taken — no more. Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei are generally used two or three at a time, forming Tung's characteristic dao ma needling, which supplements the kidney, fortifies the spleen, frees and regulates the waterways and disinhibits water to disperse swelling; it treats nephritis, enteritis, diarrhoea, vomiting, oedema of the four limbs and turbid, malodorous urine (from raised uric acid) with good results. Needling all three at once forms Tung's own dao ma and treats nephritis, cystitis and similar conditions. Master Tung's book forbids needling all three together, but in the author's clinical experience the three-needle dao ma is quite acceptable and works well.
acupoints.notes: Tongshen, Tongwei, Tongbei, Shen'er, Shuijin and Shuitong are among the few specifically effective supplementing needlings in Tung's acupuncture; in treatment, points may be chosen from them for patients of the qi-vacuity type. Red swelling on the dorsum of the foot (commonly called straw-sandal wind): bleed at the site of the problem, then needle Tongshen, Tongwei, Tongguan, Yunbai and Libai; corresponding hand and foot points may also be needled. Tongshen and Tongwei combined with the Lower Three Huang points are effective for impotence and premature ejaculation arising from kidney depletion; moxa over the needle may also be used. Master Hu added a good deal to the indications Master Tung gave for these three points, including cystitis, metritis, gastroenteritis and high blood pressure. Stomach yin and kidney yin are respectively the acquired and the innate; stomach yin is rooted in kidney yin and continually nourishes it, so that great or long-standing vacuity of stomach yin leads to exhaustion of kidney yin. Tongwei, Tongshen and Tuling may then be used as three needles forming a commanding needling, with the Lower Three Huang points added, so that the innate and the acquired are regulated together for a better result.

acupoints.name: Tongwei
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, renal nerve.
acupoints.location: 2 cun directly above Tongshen.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Fortifies the spleen and harmonises the stomach, enriches yin and subdues yang.
acupoints.indications: As for Tongshen, and also back pain, stomach pain and pain in the forearm.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1.5 cun; for dry mouth, perpendicular to 0.2 cun.
acupoints.application: Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei are generally used two or three at a time, forming Tung's characteristic dao ma needling, which supplements the kidney, fortifies the spleen, frees and regulates the waterways and disinhibits water to disperse swelling; it treats nephritis, enteritis, diarrhoea, vomiting, oedema of the four limbs and turbid, malodorous urine (from raised uric acid) with good results.
acupoints.notes: Master Hu added a good deal to the indications Master Tung gave for these three points, including cystitis, metritis, gastroenteritis and high blood pressure. Stomach yin and kidney yin are respectively the acquired and the innate; stomach yin is rooted in kidney yin and continually nourishes it, so that great or long-standing vacuity of stomach yin leads to exhaustion of kidney yin. Tongwei, Tongshen and Tuling may then be used as three needles forming a commanding needling, with the Lower Three Huang points added, so that the innate and the acquired are regulated together for a better result.

acupoints.name: Tongbei
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, renal nerve.
acupoints.location: 4 cun directly above Tongshen — that is, 2 cun above Tongwei.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Secures the kidney and banks up the origin, warms the channels and scatters cold.
acupoints.indications: As for Tongshen, and also headache, dizziness, back pain and fatigue.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1–2 cun; perpendicular to 0.3 cun resolves dry mouth at once.
acupoints.application: Needling Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei at the same time forms Tung's own dao ma and treats nephritis, cystitis and similar conditions. Master Tung's book forbids needling all three together, but in the author's clinical experience the three-needle dao ma is quite acceptable and works well.

acupoints.name: Tianhuang
acupoints.anatomy: As for Minghuang.
acupoints.location: 3 cun directly above Minghuang.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart, Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses the liver and clears the heart, boosts the kidney and supplements vacuity.
acupoints.indications: As for Minghuang; it also treats jaundice.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1.5–3 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.
acupoints.notes: Tianhuang, Minghuang and Qihuang are the Upper Three Huang points; needled together as a three-needle dao ma they are given to all liver conditions and are among the best-known and most-used points in Tung's acupuncture. Their position falls exactly along the course of the Liver channel of the twelve regular channels, so their action on the liver is cumulative, which makes them the principal points for liver disease.

acupoints.code: VIII.M.3. Thigh, medial – Upper Three Huang zone
acupoints.name: Minghuang
acupoints.anatomy: Anterior cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, general nerve of the liver, general nerve of the heart; at the surface the nerve of the heart, at the middle layer the nerve of the liver, at the deep layer the nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: Tianhuang: 3 cun directly above Minghuang. Minghuang: at the exact centre of the inner thigh. Qihuang: 3 cun directly below Minghuang.
acupoints.meridian: Tianhuang: enters the Heart, Liver and Kidney channels. Minghuang: enters the Heart, Liver and Kidney channels. Qihuang: enters the Heart, Liver and Gallbladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Tianhuang: courses the liver and clears the heart, boosts the kidney and supplements vacuity. Minghuang: calms the heart and quiets the spirit, courses the liver and disinhibits the gallbladder. Qihuang: courses the liver and disinhibits the gallbladder, dispels wind and frees the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: Tianhuang: as for Minghuang; it also treats jaundice. Minghuang: liver cancer, liver pain, cirrhosis, fatigue from insufficient liver function, enlargement of the bones, spinal periostitis, stroke with hemiplegia, leukaemia, lower back ache, blurred vision, eye pain, pain in both flanks, indigestion and flatulence from insufficient bile secretion, cardiac enlargement, chest oppression, epilepsy. Qihuang: as for Minghuang; it also treats jaundice, cholecystitis and similar conditions.
acupoints.technique: Tianhuang: perpendicular insertion, 1.5–3 cun. Minghuang: perpendicular insertion, 1–3 cun. Qihuang: perpendicular insertion, 1.5–3 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.
acupoints.notes: Tianhuang, Minghuang and Qihuang are the Upper Three Huang points, among the best-known and most-used points in Tung's acupuncture. Tung's orthodox extraordinary points do not distinguish supplementation from drainage; Master Tung held that a point acts in both directions and regulates of itself. All liver conditions, vacuity or repletion, may therefore be treated with the Upper Three Huang points. The liver governs coursing and discharge; the Liver channel encircles the genitals, reaches the lower abdomen, ascends through the diaphragm, spreads over the flanks and ribs, and meets the Du vessel at the vertex — so these points may also be applied to psychoneurotic conditions, gynaecological and urogenital conditions, and pain at the vertex. As the Upper Three Huang belong to the Liver channel, and all of Tung's liver-channel points may be used for gynaecology, they may be combined with the Fuke points to regulate menstruation. Needled together as a three-needle dao ma they are given to all liver conditions. Their position falls exactly along the course of the Liver channel of the twelve regular channels, so their action on the liver is cumulative, which makes them the principal points for liver disease.

acupoints.name: Qihuang
acupoints.anatomy: Branch nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: 3 cun directly below Minghuang.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart, Liver and Gallbladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses the liver and disinhibits the gallbladder, dispels wind and frees the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: As for Minghuang; it also treats jaundice, cholecystitis and similar conditions.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1.5–3 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation.

acupoints.code: VIII.M.1. Thigh, medial – Tuchang zone
acupoints.name: The Tuchang points
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, general nerve of the spleen, hepatic nerve, nerve of the gallbladder.
acupoints.location: Tuchang yi is 2 cun medial to Tongshen. Tuchang er is 2 cun directly above Tuchang yi. Tuchang san is 2 cun directly above Tuchang er. Tuchang si is 2 cun directly above Tuchang san. Tuchang wu is 2 cun directly above Tuchang si.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Liver channels.
acupoints.properties: Harmonises the stomach and regulates the centre, soothes the liver and disinhibits the gallbladder, fortifies the spleen and disinhibits damp.
acupoints.indications: Inflammation of the spleen, splenomegaly, dizziness, light-headedness, headache, pain in the four limbs, excess stomach acid, leukopenia, hepatitis, cholecystitis, cirrhosis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1.5–2 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness and distension with slight numbness.
acupoints.application: Tuchang is commonly used for conditions of the spleen. In practice any two or three of the points may be taken, forming a dao ma needling.
acupoints.notes: Tuchang was not published in Master Tung's original work and was added by Master Hu.
configNotes: Tuchang combined with Sanzhong and Pizhong, which are effective for tumours, treats splenomegaly.

acupoints.code: VIII.L.2. Thigh, lateral – Tongma zone
acupoints.name: Sima xia, Sima shang and Sima zhong
acupoints.anatomy: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, general nerve of the lung, branch nerve of the liver.
acupoints.location: Sima xia is 7.5 cun directly above the upper lateral border of the patella — that is, 0.5 cun above Tongshan and then 1 cun laterally.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Liver channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees and regulates the waterways, courses wind and releases the exterior.
acupoints.indications: Rib pain, chest and back pain, pleurisy, sciatica, lower back pain arising from insufficient lung function, lung disease, weak lungs, tuberculosis, lung cancer, rhinitis, tinnitus, ear inflammation, deafness, facial nerve paralysis, keratitis, asthma, mastitis, goitre, hemiplegia, psoriasis, skin conditions of every kind, acne, sprain of the lower limb, contusion of the chest.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1–3 cun.

acupoints.code: VIII.M.1. Thigh, medial – Tuchang zone
acupoints.name: Tuling
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, splenic nerve, hepatic nerve.
acupoints.location: 1 cun medial to Tongwei.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Liver channels.
acupoints.properties: Harmonises the spleen and courses the liver, frees and regulates the triple burner.
acupoints.indications: Pernicious anaemia (aplastic anaemia), leukaemia (raised or lowered white cell count).
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1–1.5 cun.
acupoints.notes: Tuling was not made public in Master Tung's original Orthodox Extraordinary Points of Tung's Acupuncture; Master Hu published it without holding anything back. It is one of Tung's 72 principal needlings. Spleen earth is the root of the acquired constitution: when spleen and stomach are robust the body is naturally healthy. The spleen also manages the blood and has the power to stop bleeding and regulate menstruation, and as Tuling is an important point on the Spleen channel it can treat bleeding conditions of every kind. In pernicious anaemia Tuling is often used to regulate. For leukaemia: as Tuling and Tuchang enter the Spleen and Liver channels they are often used for leukaemia and work better than the Upper Three Huang points; these points may also be used in alternation.
configNotes: Tuling with Tuchang treats splenomegaly. Alternatively take Tuchang yi and Tuchang er together with this point to form a triangular dao ma — also called a commanding needling — in which this point commands Tuchang yi and er and strengthens their action.

acupoints.code: VIII.L.4. Thigh, lateral – Quan zone
acupoints.name: Xiaquan, Zhongquan and Shangquan
acupoints.anatomy: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, motor nerves of the lung and the face.
acupoints.location: Xiaquan is 2.5 cun directly above the exact centre of the lateral aspect of the knee joint; Zhongquan is 2 cun above it, and Shangquan 2 cun above Zhongquan.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Liver channels.
acupoints.properties: Quickens the blood and frees the connecting vessels, moves qi and transforms stasis, frees the gates and disinhibits the joints.
acupoints.indications: Facial nerve paralysis, deviation of the mouth and eye, hemiparesis, cerebral thrombosis, sequelae of stroke.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1–2 cun.
acupoints.notes: The three Quan points of the leg are mostly taken by the balancing method of above and below, left and right: for illness on the left take the right side, and for illness on the right the left. The three Quan points combined with Sanzhong, Sancha san and Wanshun, together with points on the upper ear, can treat hardness of hearing, with results that vary from person to person. The three Quan points with Linggu, the Sihua points and Menjin can also treat gynaecological menstrual pain.

acupoints.code: VIII.L.1. Thigh, lateral – Jinqian zone
acupoints.name: Jinqian xia and Jinqian shang
acupoints.anatomy: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, motor nerve of the lung, nerve of the liver.
acupoints.location: Jinqian xia is 1 cun directly above the upper lateral corner of the patella. Jinqian shang is 1.5 cun directly above Jinqian xia.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Loosens the chest and rectifies qi, nourishes the liver and quickens the blood.
acupoints.indications: Weak lungs, epilepsy, headache, weak liver, skin allergy.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun.

acupoints.code: VIII.L.3. Thigh, lateral – Jiuli zone
acupoints.name: Xiajiuli, Shangjiuli and Zhongjiuli
acupoints.anatomy: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: As described above for Xiajiuli, Shangjiuli and Zhongjiuli.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Boosts qi and moves the blood, frees the gates and disinhibits the joints, courses the channels and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Back pain, lower back pain, spinal periostitis (bone spurs), hemiplegia, hemiparesis, neck pain, aching numb arms, leg pain, headache, dizziness, aching eyes, neuralgia, pneumonia, lung disease, abdominal distension, abdominal pain.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 2–3 cun.
acupoints.notes: Master Hu locates Shangjiuli, Zhongjiuli and Xiajiuli differently from Master Tung and from Master Lai's account, and readers should compare the versions for themselves. The three points may be used as a horizontal three-needle dao ma and are important pain-relieving points. This was also one of the key points Master Tung used in treating President Lon Nol of Cambodia for hemiplegia.

acupoints.code: VIII.A.2. Thigh, anterior – Zujie zone
acupoints.name: Jie
acupoints.anatomy: Sensitive nerve of the heart, anterior cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve.
acupoints.location: 1 cun directly above the upper lateral border of the patella, then 0.3 cun medially. Also called Zujie.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart channel.
acupoints.properties: Calms the heart and quiets the spirit, quickens the blood and transforms stagnation.
acupoints.indications: Disordered qi and blood after acupuncture, blood not returning to the channels, a lump or pain at the site of insertion, or pain following an injection given in Western medicine; injury from a fall or blow, sprained foot, pain arising from emotional shock, pain from excessive fatigue, drug allergy, food poisoning.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun.

acupoints.code: VIII.A.1. Thigh, anterior – Tonghuo zone
acupoints.name: Nei Tongguan, Nei Tongshan and Nei Tongtian
acupoints.anatomy: Femoral nerve, general nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: Nei Tongguan is 0.5 cun medial to Tongguan; for Nei Tongshan and Nei Tongtian see the individual point entries.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart channel.
acupoints.properties: Frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, boosts qi and regulates the blood.
acupoints.indications: Hemiplegia, weakness of the four limbs, nerve paralysis of the four limbs, inability to raise the arm, cardiac weakness, loss of speech after stroke, lower back pain.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.5–1 cun.
acupoints.notes: Nei Tongguan, Nei Tongshan and Nei Tongtian function much as Tongguan, Tongtian and Tongshan do, treating conditions of the circulatory system, but they are used more for weakness of the four limbs, inability to raise the arm, upper arm pain and aching lower back and back arising from the heart. They may be combined with the Upper Three Huang points, the Lower Three Huang points, Xinling, Linggu, Dabai and other major Tung points. Tung's palm diagnosis is essential: the same aching back and lower back may involve twenty or thirty possible points, and palm diagnosis decides which to use — for the heart take Nei Tongguan, for the lung Sima, for spleen and kidney Tongshen and Tongwei, for the liver the Upper Three Huang. This is the key to combining Tung's acupuncture with palm diagnosis.

acupoints.code: VIII.M.7. Thigh, medial – Shiyin zone
acupoints.name: The Shiyin points
acupoints.anatomy: Medial femoral nerve, renal nerve, principal nerve of the throat.
acupoints.location: Shiyin yi is at the centre of the medial aspect of the knee; a second point lies 2 cun below it — two points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Clears heat and disinhibits the throat, moves qi and scatters stasis.
acupoints.indications: Hoarseness, loss of voice, laryngitis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun; or oblique insertion, 0.5–0.8 cun.

acupoints.code: VIII.P.2. Thigh, posterior – Posterior Huo zone
acupoints.name: Huofu, Huoliang and Huochang
acupoints.anatomy: Posterior femoral nerve, spinal nerves, branch nerve of the heart, cranial nerves, branch nerve of the kidney, sciatic nerve.
acupoints.location: Huofu: on the back of the thigh, 3 cun directly below the centre of the gluteal crease — that is, 3 cun directly below Chengfu of the fourteen channels; locate lying prone. For Huoliang and Huochang see the individual point entries.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart, Kidney and Bladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Moves qi and quickens the blood, frees the channels and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Bone spurs of the vertebrae, sciatica, cervical bone spurs, lower back pain, back pain, contusion of the occiput, neuralgia of the cranial nerves, tight painful neck, migraine, chest oppression, nephritis, haemorrhoids, hemiplegia, coronary heart disease.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1–2.5 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness, distension, numbness and an electric sensation; sometimes an electric sensation travels up to the vertex and down to the heel.
acupoints.application: Huofu, Huoliang, Huochang and the surrounding area are mostly treated by bloodletting, combined with bloodletting at the site of the problem. Needling at the point regions of the 1-1, 2-2 and 7-7 areas may also be added.
acupoints.notes: Huofu, Huoliang and Huochang are all among Tung's 72 principal needlings; Master Hu made them public on the basis of Master Tung's teaching, making good the omission in Master Tung's original work.

acupoints.code: VIII.P.10. Thigh, posterior – Posterior Jin zone
acupoints.name: Jinfu, Jinliang and Jinchang
acupoints.anatomy: Posterior femoral nerve, nerve of the lung, branch nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: Jinfu is 2 cun lateral to Huofu; for Jinliang and Jinchang see the individual point entries.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Moves qi and quickens the blood, frees the channels and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Shoulder and arm pain, lower back pain, sciatica (specifically effective), pain in both flanks, migraine, hemiplegia, wilting patterns, back pain, haemorrhoids, acute and chronic pneumonia, chest pain, coronary heart disease.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1.5–3 cun; or spot-pricking with a bloodletting needle to release dark blood, which brings an immediate effect.
acupoints.application: The nine points Huofu, Mufu, Jinfu, Huoliang, Muliang, Jinliang, Huochang, Muchang and Jinchang are specifically effective for sciatica and lower back pain. In practice bloodletting is used more than needling; combining it with local pricking of the connecting vessels can halve the length of the course of treatment.
acupoints.notes: With the nine points described above there is no need in practice to hold rigidly to the point locations: bleed with a bloodletting needle, or needle perpendicularly, wherever there is discolouration, an abnormal appearance or a pressure-painful spot.

acupoints.code: VIII.P.6. Thigh, posterior – Posterior Mu zone
acupoints.name: Mufu, Muliang and Muchang
acupoints.anatomy: Posterior femoral nerve, accessory nerve of the liver, splenic nerve, obturator nerve.
acupoints.location: Mufu is 2 cun medial to Huofu; Muliang and Muchang are taken at their corresponding positions.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Liver channels.
acupoints.properties: Clears heat and disinhibits damp, courses the channels and quickens the blood, frees and disinhibits the waterways.
acupoints.indications: Sciatica, lower back pain, back pain, bone spurs, leg pain, rheumatoid arthritis, hepatitis, hernia, haemorrhoids, menstrual pain, enlarged prostate, constipation, diarrhoea, cystitis, urethritis, headache, coronary heart disease.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 1.5–3 cun; or spot-pricking with a bloodletting needle, which brings an immediate effect.
acupoints.notes: Mufu, Muliang, Muchang, Huofu, Huoliang and Huochang are mostly treated among Tung's points by spot-pricking with a bloodletting needle. Together with the six Anji points and with Jinfu, Jinliang and Jinchang they are collectively called the posterior femoral region (see Bloodletting Therapy in Tung's Acupuncture). Within this region, discoloured areas and pressure-painful spots may simply be scatter-pricked to bleed with a 22-gauge needle or a blood-glucose lancet; there is no need to be too exact about the point locations, as their indications are the same. None of these points was published in Master Tung's book; they were made public by Master Hu.

acupoints.code: VIII.P.1. Thigh, posterior – Anji zone
acupoints.name: The Anji points
acupoints.anatomy: Inferior gluteal nerve, spinal nerves, renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Anji yi is at the exact centre of the gluteal crease (0.5 cun medial to Chengfu of the fourteen channels). Anji er is 1 cun medial to Anji yi. Anji san is 1 cun medial to Anji er. Anji si is 1 cun lateral to Anji yi. Anji wu is 1 cun lateral to Anji si. Anji liu is 1 cun lateral to Anji wu.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Strengthens the sinews and fortifies the bones, courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: Sciatica, bone spurs of the vertebrae, bone spurs of the hip joint, back pain, lower back pain, scrofula.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 2–2.5 cun, with the needle tip kept close against the edge of the bone; or spot-pricked with a bloodletting needle to a depth of 2 cun to release dark blood.
acupoints.application: In practice any three of the Anji points are usually needled, forming a Tung dao ma to strengthen the effect — a horizontal three-needle dao ma. Master Tung did not set these points out explicitly; Master Hu made them public in his book.
configNotes: Anji combined with Erjiaoming (threaded), Wanshun yi, Sanhe, Fenshui and Huoying, or Liuwan and Huoying, works well for sciatica.

acupoints.code: IX.P.3. Ear, posterior surface – Shen'er zone
acupoints.name: Shen'er shang, Shen'er zhong and Shen'er xia
acupoints.anatomy: Great auricular nerve, lesser occipital nerve, nerve of the lung, nerve of the liver.
acupoints.location: The upper point lies on the back of the auricle at the upper border of the blood-pressure-lowering groove, one third of the way in from the medial side. For the middle and lower points see the individual point entries.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung, Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Returns yang and secures collapse, opens the orifices and rouses the spirit.
acupoints.indications: Emergency treatment of acute conditions of every kind; cardiac paralysis; emergency treatment of a heart attack; headache, dizziness, vertigo, vomiting, hepatic failure, weakness of the four limbs; emergency treatment of collapse, shock, cerebral anaemia and cerebral haemorrhage; raised cholesterol, dizziness, chest oppression, chest and back pain, high blood pressure, lower back pain, car sickness, seasickness.
acupoints.technique: Oblique insertion from above downward, 0.1–0.3 cun.
acupoints.notes: Shen'er shang, zhong and xia are arranged as a holographic projection of the body's organs. The upper point connects with the upper burner and so treats conditions of the brain, head, heart and lung. The middle point connects with the middle burner and so treats conditions of the liver, spleen, stomach and intestines. The lower point connects with the lower burner and so treats conditions of the kidney and bladder and men's and women's conditions, while also treating conditions of the upper and middle burners. In acute conditions the Shen'er points return yang and secure collapse; they can restore the pulse in a patient in extremis, and in the weak they restore strength quickly and revive vitality to remarkable effect. Master Tung did not make this point public; Master Hu supplied it. Shen'er is a key point among Tung's principal and resolving needlings. Shen'er shang, zhong and xia may be needled together as a vertical three-needle dao ma for a stronger effect.

acupoints.code: Tian'er: IX.P.5. Ear, posterior surface – Tian'er zone · Wai'er: IX.P.6. Ear, posterior surface – Wai'er zone
acupoints.name: Tian'er and Wai'er
acupoints.anatomy: Nerves of the liver and kidney.
acupoints.location: Tian'er lies on the back of the auricle, 0.2 cun lateral to Shen'er shang. Wai'er lies 0.3 cun above Jin'er and 0.2 cun toward the lateral side, or as described in the point entry.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and releases the exterior, settles and quiets the spirit.
acupoints.indications: Tian'er treats food poisoning, drug poisoning, skin allergy, dizziness, vomiting, car sickness and seasickness, and has an anti-allergic action. Wai'er treats arrhythmia, palpitations, emergency treatment of coma in stroke, headache, excessively high diastolic pressure, dizziness, and light-headedness with blurred vision.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun; or oblique insertion from above downward, 0.5 cun.
acupoints.notes: Tian'er and Wai'er were not published in Master Tung's book. They belong to Tung's 72 principal needlings and 32 resolving points, and were added by Master Hu on the basis of Master Tung's teaching. Wai'er, Tian'er and Shen'er are similar in nature and may all be regarded as supplementing points, though Tian'er acts more strongly on the skin and in resolving toxin.

acupoints.code: IX.A.1. Ear, inner surface – Five-phase ear zone
acupoints.name: Mu'er and Jin'er
acupoints.anatomy: Mu'er: the hepatic nerve. Jin'er: the nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: Mu'er lies about 0.3 cun below the transverse blood vessel in the upper half of the back of the ear. Jin'er lies at the upper end of the outer border of the back of the auricle, 0.5 cun directly above Mu'er.
acupoints.meridian: Mu'er enters the Liver channel. Jin'er enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Mu'er soothes the liver and resolves constraint, clears heat and disinhibits damp. Jin'er frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, regulates lung qi.
acupoints.indications: Mu'er treats pain in the liver region, cirrhosis, hepatomegaly, fatigue from weak liver function, and long-standing gonorrhoea. Jin'er treats constipation from insufficient lung qi, long-standing common cold, and allergic rhinitis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Among Tung's ear points, Jin'er, Mu'er, Shui'er, Huo'er and Tu'er are named for the corresponding organs and the five phases; besides their relation to those organs they also treat painful conditions. There is no need to hold rigidly to the exact location of each point: wherever a discoloured responsive mark appears nearby — dark, yellow or red — needling or bleeding at that mark will work well.
configNotes: Mu'er combined with the Upper Three Huang points (Tianhuang, Minghuang, Qihuang) and Muyan, together with bleeding at the liver-wood region of the back, is effective for cirrhosis.

acupoints.code: IX.A.1. Ear, inner surface – Five-phase ear zone
acupoints.name: Huo'er, Tu'er and Shui'er
acupoints.anatomy: Huo'er: the nerve of the heart. Tu'er: the nerve of the spleen. Shui'er: the nerve of the kidney.
acupoints.location: Huo'er is taken at the middle of the outer border of the antihelix. Tu'er lies below the liver region of the cavum conchae. Shui'er lies at the lower end of the outer border of the antihelix.
acupoints.meridian: Huo'er enters the Heart channel, Tu'er the Spleen channel, Shui'er the Kidney channel.
acupoints.properties: Huo'er rectifies qi and loosens the chest, courses and frees the connecting vessels of the heart. Tu'er fortifies the spleen and disinhibits damp. Shui'er strengthens the kidney and boosts the essence, frees and disinhibits the waterways.
acupoints.indications: Huo'er treats cardiac weakness, knee pain and aching in the four limbs. Tu'er treats neurasthenia, acute and chronic gastroenteritis, high fever and diabetes. Shui'er treats kidney depletion, lower back ache and lower abdominal distension.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Huo'er, Tu'er and Shui'er may be needled perpendicularly as a vertical three-needle Tung dao ma: Huo'er rectifies the upper burner, Tu'er regulates the middle burner and Shui'er frees the lower burner, so that the three together regulate the whole body. As with points elsewhere on the body, Tung's ear points often appear in groups of three — a defining feature of Tung's dao ma needling.

acupoints.code: IX.P.2. Ear, posterior surface – Three Er zone
acupoints.name: The three Er points
acupoints.anatomy: Nerves of the lung and kidney.
acupoints.location: Er shang is at the upper end of the outer border of the helix, Er zhong at its centre, and Er xia at its lowest end.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and releases the exterior.
acupoints.indications: Cholera, migraine, common cold, dispersing inflammation and bringing down fever.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle — two points at a time is enough.
acupoints.notes: Bleeding at Er shang has an anti-allergic action and clears the brain, brightens the eyes and lowers blood pressure. Bleeding at Er zhong disperses inflammation, brings down fever, settles the spirit and relieves pain. Bleeding at Er xia strengthens the dispersing of inflammation and the reduction of fever, clears the brain, counters allergy and lowers blood pressure. In practice the three Er points are mostly used for conditions arising from external contraction, such as headache, inflammation of the throat, and the common cold with fever.

acupoints.code: IX.A.2. Ear, inner surface – Ganyan zone
acupoints.name: The Pifu points
acupoints.anatomy: Nerve of the liver, nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: In the upper lateral part of the scapha; four points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses wind and releases the exterior, clears the liver and resolves toxin.
acupoints.indications: Urticaria, skin conditions of every kind, dispelling fatigue.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a three-edged needle, which works well.
acupoints.notes: The Pifu points are also called the Jielao points. They were omitted from Master Tung's book and supplied by Master Hu in his writings. There are four of them, and taking three as a dao ma strengthens the effect. Pifu lies close to the urticaria point of ear acupuncture, but Tung's extraordinary points appear as groups, and Tung's method mostly takes three needles as a dao ma. For skin conditions: on the ear take the lung point, endocrine point, subcortex and shenmen, then add Linggu, Huofuhai and Sima.

acupoints.code: IX.A.13. Ear, inner surface – Jiangya zone
acupoints.name: The Jiangya points
acupoints.anatomy: Nerves of the heart and kidney.
acupoints.location: On the inner border of the intertragic notch; three points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Clears and drains heart fire.
acupoints.indications: High blood pressure.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun.
acupoints.notes: Jiangya is not explicitly listed in Master Tung's book; Master Hu made it public on the basis of Master Tung's teaching. Disorders of the brain, heart, liver and kidney, diabetes and vascular conditions all affect blood pressure; for a lasting cure, use palm diagnosis to find the cause and treat it directly — only then will the result be good.

acupoints.code: IX.A.2. Ear, inner surface – Ganyan zone
acupoints.name: Muying
acupoints.anatomy: Nerve of the liver.
acupoints.location: Behind the liver region of the cavum conchae.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver channel.
acupoints.properties: Courses the liver and disinhibits the gallbladder, frees the channels and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Cirrhosis, hepatitis, liver cancer.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle, which works well.
acupoints.notes: In treating cirrhosis, ear points, body points and bloodletting areas are used in combination. Muying was not disclosed in Master Tung's original work; Master Hu made it public on the basis of what Master Tung taught day to day.

acupoints.code: IX.A.4. Ear, inner surface – Zhongliu zone
acupoints.name: The Zhongliu points
acupoints.anatomy: Nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: On the outer border of the earlobe; six points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Moves qi and breaks blood, dispels wind and transforms stagnation.
acupoints.indications: Malignant tumour, cancerous swelling, abscesses and flat-abscesses, lymphatic tumour, scrofula.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Zhongliu is not listed in Master Tung's book; Master Hu made it public on the basis of Master Tung's teaching. Besides this point, the well-known tumour-related points in Tung's acupuncture include Waisanguan and Sanzhong. Tumour points are generally combined with the key qi-freeing and qi-regulating points — Linggu, Dabai and Sima — and then with points relating to the organ involved: for a uterine tumour add the Fuke points on the hand, for a liver tumour the Upper Three Huang points on the leg (Tianhuang, Minghuang, Qihuang). Anyone with a tumour must, alongside treatment with Tung's acupuncture, observe a number of dietary restrictions, avoiding duck, goose, seafood, alcohol, aubergine, peanuts, pork head skin, bamboo shoots and the like.

acupoints.code: Jiehe: IX.A.7. Ear, inner surface – Jiehe zone · Feijin: IX.A.9. Ear, inner surface – Feijin zone
acupoints.name: Jiehe and Feijin
acupoints.anatomy: Nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: Jiehe lies on the inner side of the cavum conchae, lateral to the opening of the external auditory canal; three points in all. Feijin lies at the centre of the lung region; two points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Dispels wind and releases the exterior, enriches the lung and nourishes yin.
acupoints.indications: Pulmonary tuberculosis, pneumonia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1 cun.

acupoints.code: IX.P.1. Ear, posterior surface – Jiazhuangxianzhong zone
acupoints.name: The Jiazhuangxianzhong points
acupoints.anatomy: Nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: On the lower inner border of the back of the ear; three points in all.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung channel.
acupoints.properties: Moves qi and scatters stasis, clears the throat and disinhibits the larynx.
acupoints.indications: Goitre, palpitations.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1 cun.
acupoints.application: This group may be used as a dao ma needling or bled, either of which multiplies the effect.
acupoints.notes: Jiazhuangxianzhong, Xiaxin and Jiehe are not explicitly listed in Master Tung's book; Master Hu made them public on the basis of Master Tung's teaching. For goitre, ear points are not used alone but mostly combined as follows: Linggu, Xinling, Sanzhong and Sima, with bloodletting at the site; Xinling, the Sihua points and Sanzhong, with bloodletting at the nine Hou'e points; Xinling yi, Sihua shang, Sima, Sanzhong and the eighteen star points, with bloodletting at the site; Sima, Sanzhong, Tongguan and Tongshan, with bloodletting at the site.

acupoints.code: IX.A.12. Ear, inner surface – Xiangjin zone
acupoints.name: Xiangjin
acupoints.anatomy: Branch nerves of the heart and lung.
acupoints.location: About one third of the way up the outer aspect of the earlobe.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Courses the sinews and disinhibits the joints, quickens the blood and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Aching neck, tight painful neck.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2 cun.
acupoints.notes: Xiangjin was not made public by Master Tung; Master Hu set it out in his writings. In practice it is not a principal point: stiff painful neck is mostly treated on the hands and feet — Shizhen and Wanshun xia on the hand, Shenguan, Zhengjin, Zhengzong and Renhuang on the foot. But when a dark spot appears over Xiangjin, bleeding it with a bloodletting needle works better still.

acupoints.code: IX.A.10. Ear, inner surface – Xingfen zone
acupoints.name: Xingfen
acupoints.anatomy: Cranial nerves.
acupoints.location: As described above for Xingfen.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Clears and drains heart fire, enriches and supplements the liver.
acupoints.indications: Listlessness and low spirits, excessive sleepiness, neurasthenia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.application: This point lifts the spirits and rouses the brain; combined with Shen'er shang the effect is doubled.
acupoints.notes: Xingfen, Pifu and Shen'er all lift the spirits and rouse the brain; after tiring work, needling any one of the three relieves fatigue. Xingfen was not listed in Master Tung's original work and was later made public by Master Hu on the basis of Master Tung's regular teaching.

acupoints.code: X.Ve.1. Vertex – Touhui zone
acupoints.name: Zhenghui
acupoints.anatomy: Zhenghui: frontal nerve, general nerve of the brain. Qianhui: frontal nerve, accessory nerve of the brain. Houhui: greater occipital nerve, general nerve of the brain, spinal nerves.
acupoints.location: Zhenghui: 0.5 cun behind the exact centre of the vertex — that is, 0.5 cun behind Baihui of the fourteen channels. Qianhui: 1.5 cun in front of Zhenghui. Houhui: 1.5 cun behind Zhenghui.
acupoints.meridian: Zhenghui: enters the Heart and Lung channels and the Du vessel. Qianhui: enters the Heart and Lung channels and the Du vessel. Houhui: enters the Liver and Lung channels and the Du vessel.
acupoints.properties: Zhenghui: clears the heart and opens the orifices, frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels. Qianhui: rouses the brain and opens the orifices, frees the channels and quickens the blood. Houhui: courses and frees the channels and connecting vessels, quickens the blood and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Zhenghui: trembling of the four limbs, wind patterns of every kind, bodily weakness, childhood fright wind, deviation of the eye and mouth, hemiplegia, loss of speech after stroke, weakness of the legs, wilting patterns, autonomic dysregulation. Qianhui: dizziness, blurred vision, distension in the head, neurasthenia, coma after stroke, hemiplegia. Houhui: cerebral congestion, headache, dizziness, pain in the vertebrae, tuberculosis of bone, loss of speech after stroke, hemiplegia, nerve paralysis.
acupoints.technique: Zhenghui: needle to a depth of 0.1–0.3 cun. Qianhui: perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun; or spot-pricking with a bloodletting needle, which takes effect at once. Houhui: perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Zhenghui: soreness and distension. Qianhui: distension. Houhui: soreness and distension.
acupoints.application: Spot-pricking Zhenghui to bleed with a bloodletting needle lowers blood pressure; adding bloodletting at Liuwan treats nosebleed. Qianhui can bring an unconscious patient round at once. Zhouyuan, Zhoulun and Zhoukun are the key points for wilting weakness of the four limbs; combined with Zhenghui, Qianhui and Houhui they treat stroke and hemiplegia.
acupoints.notes: Zhenghui is by no means the same as Baihui: the location differs slightly, the indications differ a little, and the effect differs more. Zhenghui, Qianhui and Houhui form a dao ma; in treating stroke with hemiplegia they may be threaded obliquely from one point to the next, with Zhouyuan and Zhoukun 1.5 cun to the side likewise threaded obliquely and electro-acupuncture added to strengthen the effect, which works well. The three Hui points with Zhenjing and Xinling treat insomnia from neurasthenia; bloodletting from the cervical vertebrae to the coccyx may be added, together with needling Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei. Needling or bleeding the three Hui points on the head, with Zhenjing, the Upper Three Huang points, Sanzhong, Zhengjin and Zhengzong added, is effective for Parkinson's disease. For neurasthenia: needle Shuijin, Shuitong, the Lower Three Huang points, Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei.

acupoints.code: X.Ve.2. Vertex – Touyuan zone
acupoints.name: Zhouyuan
acupoints.anatomy: Zhouyuan: frontal nerve, nerve of the lung. Zhoukun: greater occipital nerve, nerve of the lung. Zhoulun: frontal nerve, nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: Zhouyuan: 1.5 cun to the side of Zhenghui. Zhoukun: 1.5 cun directly behind Zhouyuan. Zhoulun: 1.5 cun directly in front of Zhouyuan.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Bladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Zhouyuan: dispels wind and frees the orifices, courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels. Zhoukun: frees the orifices and rouses the brain, courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels. Zhoulun: frees the connecting vessels and boosts the brain.
acupoints.indications: Zhouyuan: asthma, sciatica, back pain, aching pain in the four limbs, weakness of the four limbs, hemiplegia. Zhoukun: as for Zhouyuan, and also neuralgia of the cranial nerves. Zhoulun: as for Zhouyuan, and also brain tumour, headache and dizziness.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Zhouyuan: soreness and distension. Zhoukun: distension. Zhoulun: soreness and distension.
acupoints.application: In practice the principle is to take the right side for illness on the left and the left side for illness on the right. Zhoukun and Zhoulun are likewise taken by the rule of left for right and right for left, to treat weakness of the four limbs or the sequelae of stroke. Zhouyuan, Zhoukun and Zhoulun may be used as a vertical three-needle Tung dao ma, whose effects multiply and double the result.

acupoints.name: Zhoukun
acupoints.anatomy: Greater occipital nerve, nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: 1.5 cun directly behind Zhouyuan.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Bladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees the orifices and rouses the brain, courses the channels and quickens the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: As for Zhouyuan, and also neuralgia of the cranial nerves.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle.

acupoints.name: Zhoulun
acupoints.anatomy: Frontal nerve, nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: 1.5 cun directly in front of Zhouyuan.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Bladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees the connecting vessels and boosts the brain.
acupoints.indications: As for Zhouyuan, and also brain tumour, headache and dizziness.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle.
acupoints.application: Zhoukun and Zhoulun are taken by the rule of left for right and right for left, to treat weakness of the four limbs or the sequelae of stroke. Zhouyuan, Zhoukun and Zhoulun may be used as a vertical three-needle Tung dao ma, whose effects multiply and double the result.

acupoints.name: Qianhui
acupoints.anatomy: Frontal nerve, accessory nerve of the brain.
acupoints.location: 1.5 cun in front of Zhenghui.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels and the Du vessel.
acupoints.properties: Rouses the brain and opens the orifices, frees the channels and quickens the blood.
acupoints.indications: Dizziness, blurred vision, distension in the head, neurasthenia, coma after stroke, hemiplegia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun; or spot-pricking with a bloodletting needle, which takes effect at once.
acupoints.application: This point can bring an unconscious patient round at once.
acupoints.notes: Zhenghui, Qianhui and Houhui with Zhenjing and Xinling treat insomnia from neurasthenia; bloodletting from the cervical vertebrae to the coccyx may be added, together with needling Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei. Needling or bleeding the three Hui points on the head, with Zhenjing, the Upper Three Huang points, Sanzhong, Zhengjin and Zhengzong added, is effective for Parkinson's disease. For neurasthenia: needle Shuijin, Shuitong, the Lower Three Huang points, Tongshen, Tongwei and Tongbei.

acupoints.name: Houhui
acupoints.anatomy: Greater occipital nerve, general nerve of the brain, spinal nerves.
acupoints.location: 1.5 cun behind Zhenghui.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Lung channels and the Du vessel.
acupoints.properties: Courses and frees the channels and connecting vessels, quickens the blood and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: Cerebral congestion, headache, dizziness, pain in the vertebrae, tuberculosis of bone, loss of speech after stroke, hemiplegia, nerve paralysis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle.
acupoints.application: Zhouyuan, Zhoulun and Zhoukun are the key points for wilting weakness of the four limbs; combined with Zhenghui, Qianhui and Houhui they treat stroke and hemiplegia.

acupoints.code: X.P.2. Head, back – Zongshu zone
acupoints.name: Zongshu
acupoints.anatomy: Greater occipital nerve, dantian nerve.
acupoints.location: On the back of the head, 0.8 cun below Naohu.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels and the Du vessel.
acupoints.properties: Rectifies qi and loosens the chest, frees the gates and opens the orifices.
acupoints.indications: Vomiting, neck pain, chest oppression, weakness of the heart, cholera, speaking without voice.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun; spot-pricking with a bloodletting needle works best.
acupoints.application: Spot-pricking this point to bleed with a bloodletting needle treats liver cholera.
acupoints.notes: The back of the neck and the back are generally more hazardous, so in these areas Tung's extraordinary points are mostly treated by bloodletting with a 22-gauge needle or a blood-glucose lancet, to avoid risk.

acupoints.code: X.A.1. Head, front – Eyebrow zone
acupoints.name: Zhenjing
acupoints.anatomy: Supratrochlear nerve, branches of the facial nerve, cranial nerves, nerve of the heart.
acupoints.location: 0.5 cun directly above the midpoint between the inner ends of the eyebrows.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart channel and the Ren vessel.
acupoints.properties: Clears the heart and settles spasm.
acupoints.indications: Mental derangement, trembling of the four limbs, aching weakness of both legs, nerve paralysis of the four limbs, insomnia, night terrors in children, headache and dizziness with a heavy distended feeling from inflammation of the nasal cavity; frontal headache and vomiting arising from heart disease.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun; or oblique insertion from above downward, 0.2–0.5 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Soreness and distension, extending to the tip of the nose and up to the vertex.

acupoints.code: X.A.1. Head, front – Eyebrow zone
acupoints.name: Shangli
acupoints.anatomy: Shangli: ocular nerve, facial nerve, auriculotemporal nerve. Sifu yi: ocular nerve, facial nerve, auriculotemporal nerve, nerve of the lung. Sifu er: ocular nerve, facial nerve, auriculotemporal nerve.
acupoints.location: Shangli: 0.5 cun directly above the inner end of the eyebrow. Sifu yi: 0.5 cun directly above the outer end of the eyebrow. Sifu er: 0.5 cun directly above the exact midpoint of the eyebrow.
acupoints.meridian: Shangli: enters the Heart and Gallbladder channels. Sifu yi: enters the Lung channel. Sifu er: enters the Lung and Gallbladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Shangli: frees the channels and scatters wind, soothes the sinews and quickens the connecting vessels. Sifu yi: soothes the sinews and quickens the connecting vessels. Sifu er: frees the channels and scatters wind, settles spasm and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Distending pain from raised intraocular pressure, aching pain, dull pain, headache, facial nerve paralysis, deviation of the mouth and eye, vomiting, nausea and regurgitation, abdominal distension, mental derangement.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun; or spot-pricking to bleed with a bloodletting needle, which works outstandingly well.
acupoints.application: Taking Shangli, Sifu yi and Sifu er together and spot-pricking them with a bloodletting needle to release dark blood works better still.
acupoints.notes: Suitable points among Tung's extraordinary points on the face are often needled with a 36-gauge 0.5-cun needle for cosmetic effect and to prevent wrinkles; points on the forehead can prevent and treat forehead lines.

acupoints.code: X.A.2. Head, front – Nose zone
acupoints.name: Zhengben
acupoints.anatomy: Crossing nerve of the lung.
acupoints.location: Lying supine or sitting upright, with the head tilted slightly back: at the tip of the nose, feel for the small cartilages to left and right — the point is in the depression between them.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Heart and Lung channels.
acupoints.properties: Rectifies qi and diffuses the lung, frees the orifices and boosts the brain.
acupoints.indications: Allergic rhinitis, treating possession by malign spirits, declining mental power, weakness of the lung.
acupoints.technique: Needle to a depth of 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.application: Take care not to injure the cartilage.
acupoints.notes: Zhengben is strongly stimulating; a 36-gauge 0.5-cun needle may be used, and the patient should draw as full a breath as possible during insertion — a full breath makes it less painful and improves the result.

acupoints.code: X.A.4. Head, front – Touma zone
acupoints.name: Majinshui
acupoints.anatomy: Majinshui: masseteric nerve, renal nerve, accessory branch nerve of the lung. Makuaishui: masseteric nerve, renal nerve, bladder nerve.
acupoints.location: Majinshui: from the outer canthus down to the lower border of the zygomatic bone, then 0.4 cun laterally — that is, 0.4 cun lateral to Quanliao of the fourteen channels. Makuaishui: 0.4 cun directly below Majinshui.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung, Kidney and Bladder channels.
acupoints.properties: Majinshui: frees and regulates the waterways, courses wind and frees the connecting vessels. Makuaishui: frees and disinhibits the lower burner, courses and frees the channels and connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: Majinshui: kidney stones, acute lumbar sprain, nephritis, lower back pain, back pain, rhinitis, wrenched qi (pain felt on breathing). Makuaishui: bladder stones, cystitis, frequent urination, pain in the lumbar vertebrae, bone spurs, sinusitis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.2–0.3 cun.
acupoints.needleFeeling: Majinshui: soreness and distension. Makuaishui: local soreness and distension.
acupoints.application: Taking Majinshui and Makuaishui together, needling both at once, forms Tung's characteristic kneeling-horse needling and doubles the effect.
acupoints.notes: In the names Majinshui and Makuaishui, ma means quick; jin (metal) is the lung, which governs qi, and shui (water) is the kidney, which governs water — so the names themselves show that these points also treat wrenched qi, nephritis and oedema.

acupoints.code: X.A.5. Head, front – Toukuai zone
acupoints.name: Fukuai
acupoints.anatomy: Renal nerve, nerve of the six bowels.
acupoints.location: 0.5 cun lateral to the lower border of the nose, then 0.5 cun directly upward.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Stomach channels.
acupoints.properties: Drains fire and scatters wind, clears and disinhibits the lower burner.
acupoints.indications: Abdominal distension, abdominal pain, hernia, stomach pain, blocked nose.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.3 cun.
acupoints.notes: In naming Tung's extraordinary points, the characters ma (horse, meaning quick) and kuai (fast) both indicate that the point takes effect rapidly.

acupoints.code: X.A.3. Head, front – Shuijin – Shuitong zone
acupoints.name: Shuitong
acupoints.anatomy: Renal nerve.
acupoints.location: Shuitong: 0.5 cun below the corner of the mouth. Shuijin: 0.5 cun obliquely medial to Shuitong.
acupoints.meridian: Shuitong: enters the Spleen, Kidney and Stomach channels. Shuijin: enters the Spleen and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Shuitong: harmonises the spleen and stomach, banks up the kidney and secures the root. Shuijin: fortifies the spleen and boosts the kidney, warms the channels and frees the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: Rheumatic kidney disease, fatigue from insufficient kidney function, dizziness, blurred vision, kidney vacuity, lower back pain, acute lumbar sprain, wrenched qi, back pain, dry mouth, gastric ulcer, duodenal ulcer, abdominal distension and flatulence.
acupoints.technique: Shuitong: oblique insertion, 0.5 cun; or perpendicular insertion, 0.3 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle. Shuijin: perpendicular insertion, 0.2–0.5 cun. Oblique insertion: from Shuijin toward Shuitong, the needle tip threading straight through to Qikuai.
acupoints.application: Shuijin and Shuitong are specifically effective kidney-supplementing points. When the colour near the two points is abnormal, needling or spot-pricking the discoloured bluish vessel or mark works best. In practice the two are mostly taken together as Tung's characteristic kneeling-horse needling, or with Qikuai added to form a dao ma — Tung's horizontal three-needle dao ma — for a still greater effect. For aching lower back of the kidney-vacuity type, needle both Shuijin and Shuitong; they are among the qi-supplementing points of Tung's acupuncture. Whether the cough comes from counterflow ascent of lung qi or the wheezing from the kidney failing to grasp qi, Shuijin and Shuitong can downbear any counterflow of qi.
acupoints.notes: Master Tung's original work places Shuitong 0.4 cun below the corner of the mouth; Master Hu's correction to 0.5 cun is followed here as closer to Master Tung's intent. Dao ma needling means taking three needles: dao ma is a horse falling — a horse missing one leg falls, so three legs remain. Kneeling-horse needling means taking two needles — a kneeling horse stands on two. Kneeling-horse and dao ma needling are defined by the number of needles used.

acupoints.meridian: Enters the Spleen and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Fortifies the spleen and boosts the kidney, warms the channels and frees the connecting vessels.
acupoints.indications: As for Shuitong.

acupoints.code: X.A.2. Head, front – Nose zone
acupoints.name: Biyi
acupoints.anatomy: Nerves of the lung, kidney and spleen.
acupoints.location: In the groove at the upper end of the centre of the ala of the nose.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Lung and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees the channels and resolves constraint, courses the sinews and disinhibits the joints.
acupoints.indications: Neuralgias of every kind arising from kidney depletion, hemiplegia, aching pain in the four limbs, painful tongue, stiff tongue, tight tongue, sore throat, distension in the head, migraine, dizziness with blurred vision, facial paralysis.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.1–0.2 cun.
acupoints.application: Yuhuo governs blood conditions and Biyi governs qi conditions; taking both together forms a kneeling-horse needling that treats qi and blood at once and doubles the effect.
acupoints.notes: Biyi frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels strongly and is much used for pain of every kind arising from qi vacuity or qi constraint. Combined with Shen'er, Zhengben and Pifu it also lifts the spirits, rouses the brain and dispels fatigue. Taking the point on both sides with Zhenjing, together with bloodletting on either side of the ala of the nose, is effective for a blocked nose. Where the constitution is being regulated, the needle should not be retained for more than thirty minutes.

acupoints.code: X.P.1. Head, back – Touzhou zone
acupoints.name: Zhouling
acupoints.anatomy: Greater occipital nerve, cranial nerves, renal nerve.
acupoints.location: 1.5 cun lateral to Zhoushui yi.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees the channels and quickens the connecting vessels, scatters stasis and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Migraine, sciatica, lower back pain, leg pain, calming the spirit, hemiplegia.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun. Spot-pricking to bleed with a bloodletting needle treats headache and heel pain.
acupoints.notes: Houhui stands for the head and Zhoushui, at the high bone of the occiput, for the buttocks, so that the area forms a holographic projection of the back of the body — which is why Zhoushui can treat pain of the lumbar vertebrae. Zhouling lies beside it and so treats sciatica and lower back pain.

acupoints.code: X.P.1. Head, back – Touzhou zone
acupoints.name: Zhoutian
acupoints.anatomy: Greater occipital nerve, renal nerve.
acupoints.location: 1.5 cun lateral to Zhouling.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Soothes the channels and quickens the blood, transforms stasis and relieves pain.
acupoints.indications: Trigeminal neuralgia, sciatica, migraine.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle, which works well.
acupoints.application: Zhouling, Zhoutian and Zhoushui taken together as a horizontal three-needle dao ma work better still for sciatica; adding points in the 1-1 or 2-2 regions of the hand improves the result further. Most of Tung's points on the head can treat hemiplegia after stroke; in practice three needles may be inserted transversely from front to back — the line of Qianhui, Zhenghui and Houhui, and then the line of Zhoulun, Zhouyuan and Zhoukun 1.5 cun to the side — with electro-acupuncture added. Over several courses this works well for hemiplegia. All the points on the head may be taken in this way.
acupoints.notes: Zhouling, Zhoutian and Zhouyin were not made public in Master Tung's book; Master Hu set them out on the basis of Master Tung's regular teaching, without holding anything back.

acupoints.code: X.P.1. Head, back – Touzhou zone
acupoints.name: Zhouyin
acupoints.anatomy: Greater occipital nerve, renal nerve.
acupoints.location: 1.5 cun in front of Zhoutian.
acupoints.meridian: Enters the Liver and Kidney channels.
acupoints.properties: Frees the sinews and disinhibits the joints, quickens the blood and transforms stasis.
acupoints.indications: As for Zhoutian.
acupoints.technique: Perpendicular insertion, 0.3–0.5 cun; or spot-pricked to bleed with a bloodletting needle, which takes effect at once.
acupoints.notes: Zhouyin, like Zhouling and Zhoutian, was made public by Master Hu on the basis of Master Tung's teaching. Tung's acupuncture is said to comprise more than seven hundred and forty points, yet Master Tung's own book, and the works of Master Lai and Master Yang, give only a hundred and seventy. Dr Hu Wen-chih set out nearly a hundred of the more important points that Master Tung had taught in the ordinary course of practice, doing much to make good the loss to Tung's orthodox extraordinary points — a selflessness that deserves recognition and praise.
